articles.content: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests | MIT Technology Review Skip to Content In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth. Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land . As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records. That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba , hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest. The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife. Filling in the gaps Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees , after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way? While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs , Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. Rather than despair, she turned to restoration. Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land. Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says. But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies. Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary. In 2009, she published an encouraging paper showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow. In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow. In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence. The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says. For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees. Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases. In the Gustavia -dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root. These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees. To plant or not to plant Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015. She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests. Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a 2016 paper in Nature showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun. Then, in a 2022 study published by the Royal Society, Dent and colleagues showed that locations such as Barro Colorado are among the best-case scenarios for what can be achieved without planting a single seed. Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which help tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness and abundance within a few decades. Using data from Panama and Brazil, Dent published a follow-up in 2024 showing that plots with as little as 35% of tree cover can regenerate as forest. “Having these long-term mapped forest plots is really valuable,” says Liza Comita, a professor of tropical forest ecology at Yale University, who is collaborating with Dent on projects that translate her findings into action. “It provides this really nice research infrastructure where you can build projects on top of that.” In Panama, Dent works with nonprofits and carbon-crediting schemes to fast-track recovery. They’ve mapped corridors to reconnect forest fragments and made plans to reintroduce animals in “silent forests” that have lost much of their wildlife. They’re also working to replant tree species that can accelerate growth—what Comita calls assisted natural regeneration. Leaving plots alone may seem like the simpler option, but it can’t be done everywhere, says Dent. Many sites are too degraded. Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which helps tree cover regain old-growth ­levels of richness. The two are working with the London-based carbon-crediting startup Ponterra to develop solutions for a region of southern Panama where remnant forests line the edges of abandoned ranches. Such sites almost always need some intervention, Comita explains. Many demand hands-on actions, such as enrichment planting. Today, the questions projects like Ponterra are asking are closer to her own research, says Dent. For instance, they want to understand if solitary standing trees, often left by ranchers to shade cows, help sites regenerate faster. Those insights can help Ponterra sell high-quality credits and avoid the embarrassing pitfalls that can lead fresh plantations to literally go up in smoke. While credits can be bought for as little as $5 per metric ton, corporate giants such as Microsoft—one of Ponterra’s clients—have paid more than 10 times as much for high-quality removal. There are plenty of places where a level of natural regeneration can work well. So far, millions of hectares of rainforest are naturally regenerating in Brazil, according to the Brazilian Restoration and Reforestation Observatory. Still, Dent is mystified as to why the people in charge of large-scale projects continue to think the best solution is the one that imposes humans’ will on the landscape. The conversation may be shifting. As droughts hit Latin America, policymakers and carbon creditors might be forced to face the shortcomings of cookie-cutter plantations. “You have much reduced resilience in the system when it comes to extreme events like droughts or floods or extreme heat or pathogens,” Dent says. The coming year’s “mega El Niño” could be a moment of reckoning, she says: “I think there’s an increasing recognition that we can’t just plant trees. We have to rebuild a system.” Matthew Ponsford is a freelance reporter based in London. articles.title: Why the worst El Niño killed millions – and how we can avoid a repeat
articles.summary: The world hasn't experienced an El Niño this strong since the 1870s, when it sparked a terrible global famine. Are we better prepared this time?
articles.content: Why the worst El Niño killed millions – and how we can avoid a repeat | New Scientist Advertisement Subscribe now A wood engraving captures the scene of a mother selling her children for bread during the 1877 famine in China The Granger Collection/Alamy To read of the great famine that swept the globe in the 1870s is to read of a hellscape worse than your imagination could conjure. In China, India, Brazil and beyond, after years of drought and failed harvests, millions died of starvation. People rioted, begged, stole, murdered for food. They knowingly ate diseased animals, tree roots, mud, pets and strips of leather in desperate bids to stay alive. By many contemporary accounts, cannibalism was rife. Children were sold or sacrificed for a meal. Corpses were bricked into their homes by family members to stop them being pillaged and eaten by hungry neighbours. Bodies littered the roadsides. The chaos didn’t stop at just hunger. Those who had fled famine took shelter in filthy camps and shanty towns, which were then struck by deadly outbreaks of cholera, smallpox and other diseases. In China, when winter came and there was no money for fuel, people burned their own houses. The desperate then crowded together in underground pits for warmth. Society all but fell apart. Once the poor had died in a region, the wealthy succumbed. Read more Super El Niño could lead to mega CO2 emissions from fires in Indonesia When the rains finally returned, there was barely anyone left to sow the crops. The total death toll across India, China and Brazil between 1876 and 1879 is estimated at 20 million to 30 million. Globally, there may have been 50 million deaths. As historian Mike Davis writes in the book Late Victorian Holocausts , this was a disaster of “truly planetary magnitude”. Advertisement The root cause of this catastrophe? A supersized El Niño event, which released vast amounts of heat from the ocean into the atmosphere, triggering severe disruption to global weather patterns. Discovering El Niño Of course, scientists in 1877 weren’t aware of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation cycle. There was rudimentary meteorological data collection under way: sea-surface temperatures were collated, rain gauges were monitored, barometric pressure was observed. Scientists knew something strange was happening to global weather patterns, but the cause was far from clear. In the immediate aftermath of the 1877/78 El Niño, many researchers were convinced sunspots were to blame. “As a scientific topic, this was the Stone Ages for El Niño. No one in the scientific community knew about this problem. The only ones who probably knew about it were Peruvian fishermen,” says Michael McPhaden at the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Emergency briefing on the nature and climate crisis Hear from three of the world’s leading climate scientists at New Scientist Live 2026 Find out more It wasn’t until the 1920s that physicist Gilbert Walker first identified the seesaw of atmospheric pressure across the tropics, known as the Southern Oscillation. Then, in 1969, meteorologist Jacob Bjerknes connected changing sea-surface temperatures in the Pacific to the Southern Oscillation and mapped out the global dynamics of an El Niño. That was the “big bang” for El Niño research, says McPhaden, ushering in the idea that with the right data and equipment, El Niños could be identified in real time – and even predicted in advance. Imperial failure Of course, El Niños had occurred before 1877. Authorities in China and India held grain reserves for when monsoon rains failed. But the 1877/78 El Niño was stronger than anything that had come before. Boyin Huang , also at NOAA, and his colleagues have used modern data analysis methods to estimate just how strong it was. The analysis uses sea-surface data from ships, buoys and modern floats, organised to reconstruct a temperature record stretching back to 1850. “From our data reconstruction, we did find the El Niño signature, and it is a very strong El Niño,” he says. The strength of an El Niño is usually measured by how far sea-surface temperatures in a specific region of the tropical Pacific have deviated from normal. In 1877/88, after accounting for the background ocean warming trend observed since then, temperatures in the Nino3 index were 2.88°C above average, Huang’s research indicates. This suggests it was among the strongest – if not the strongest – event in modern history. Read more Super El Niño set to cause ‘terribly dangerous’ drought in the Amazon The 1877/78 El Niño resulted in droughts around the world. The situation was most acute in northern China, which suffered its worst drought in 300 years, in north-eastern Brazil, India, South Africa and northern Africa. In some of these locations, drought had begun even before El Niño hit, triggered in part by unusually cool conditions in the tropical Pacific immediately before the arrival of El Niño. The result was three or more years of very little rain, and repeated crop failures. But the impact of the droughts was made far worse by the ineptitude of governments’ official response. In India, colonial rulers continued to collect taxes, hoard grain and enforce food exports to England despite widespread starvation among local populations. In China, corrupt officials raided grain supplies, and poor transport links made it difficult to get food to those who needed it. Water levels on the Grand Canal, a vital transport link into the hardest hit Shanxi province, dropped so low that it was unnavigable. There were no railways, and the mountain roads into Shanxi thronged with bandits who killed the livestock being used to transport grain before they could reach the starving. “Because of the workings of the imperial economy at that time, those droughts translated into colossal famines with millions of dead in India and China,” says Richard Seager at Columbia University in New York. The return of a monster For more than a century, the 1877/78 El Niño has stood as the strongest in history. But this year, a super El Niño has once again erupted in the tropical Pacific, and on current forecasts it looks set to outstrip even 1877/78 in its intensity. Current predictions forecast sea-surface temperatures in the El Niño region of the Pacific Ocean peaking 4°C above normal in November. The big difference this time is that we already know the event is occurring. Scientists have been able to forecast El Niño events months in advance since the 1990s. That affords governments, emergency services, farmers and citizens vital time to prepare by increasing water storage, sowing drought-resistant crops, improving warning systems, restoring flood defences and more. “Being forewarned is being forearmed. If you know something is coming and it can have really damaging impacts, you have some choices to make,” says McPhaden. Models began to hint at a coming El Niño in February 2026, and by April there were clear signs that a strong event was looming. That gave governments a three-month head start before the El Niño even began, and at least six months of warning before impacts would be felt. Improvements in El Niño forecasting, with the help of AI, mean it could soon be possible to predict a coming El Niño two years in advance, says McPhaden. “The longer you have to prepare, the more options you have. And the better off you may be in the end,” he says. Galapagos corals suggest climate change drives stronger El Niños Coral records from the Galapagos Islands indicate El Niños have been gathering strength over the past 40 years, in line with rising global temperatures But although there are prospects to improve El Niño forecasts even further, it comes at a time when US federal funding for climate research and global aid has been severely curtailed. In January 2025, US President Donald Trump issued an executive order shutting down a US-funded famine early warning system. Six months later it was reinstated, but data reporting since then has been patchy, news reports suggest . The US has also severely cut funding to the World Food Programme, which provides emergency food relief. Other high-income countries, including the UK, have also scaled back their overseas aid budgets in recent years. Meanwhile, the US war with Iran and blockade in the Strait of Hormuz has pushed up fuel and fertiliser prices , while Russia’s war in Ukraine has curtailed the global wheat trade. This El Niño “is happening at a very bad time”, says Seager. Nevertheless, early preparation, coupled with a more comprehensive global trading network, better transport links and modern agricultural methods, means the world is much, much better prepared to deal with a monster El Niño than it was 150 years ago. “We have much better public health systems,” says McPhaden. “We have much better understanding of disease and disease controls. And we have humanitarian organisations, and we have social safety nets, that will not let 50 million people die like happened in 1877-78.” Topics: drought / El Niño More from New Scientist Explore the latest news, articles and features Environment Rising water is creating inland ghost forests in the US News Environment Record El Niño threatens Great Barrier Reef with ecological shift News Environment The world may never go back to how it was after this monster El Niño News Environment Cameraless photography creates unique images of environmental change Regulars Popular articles Trending New Scientist articles Tattoos could be turned on and off with light Can we harness the brain’s deep-cleaning system to prevent Alzheimer’s? articles.title: Neutrino physicist wins 2026 Nobel Physics Prize
articles.summary: Francis Halzen of University of Wisconsin-Madison led development of IceCube Neutrino Observatory.
articles.content: Neutrino physicist wins 2026 Nobel Physics Prize - Ars Technica Skip to content Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Francis Halzen, a physicist at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.” Halzen spearheaded the development and construction of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, enabling physicists to capture high-energy neutrinos created in the distant universe. “It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” Halzen said during a news conference in Stockholm, Sweden, speaking by phone from Italy. While the Nobel was awarded to Halzen, he emphasized that his work was the result of a “large collaboration” with other researchers. “This reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in this project when really no respectable conservative physicist would have joined me. But many talented people did, and that’s why I’m here,” he said . “I am shocked and absolutely delighted that Francis was awarded the Nobel this year,” said particle physicist Danielle Norcini of Johns Hopkins University in a statement. “He is the scientific visionary and driving force behind [IceCube]. It has transformed our understanding of the universe by detecting the first high-energy neutrinos from beyond our galaxy, opening an entirely new field of neutrino astronomy. The experiment is the extraordinary achievement of hundreds of scientists, engineers, and collaborators, but Francis was the person who dreamed big enough to imagine an experiment of this scale and then relentlessly pushed to make it a reality.” Ghost particles As previously reported , neutrinos travel near the speed of light. John Updike’s 1960 poem, “ Cosmic Gall ,” pays tribute to the two most defining features of neutrinos: They have no charge, and for decades, physicists believed they had no mass (they actually have a teeny bit of mass). Neutrinos are the most abundant subatomic particle in the universe, but they very rarely interact with any type of matter. We are constantly being bombarded every second by millions of these tiny particles, yet they pass right through us without our even noticing. That’s why Isaac Asimov dubbed them “ghost particles.” Mark Pearce, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics, presents the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics. Credit: Patrick Lundin Mark Pearce, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics, presents the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics. Credit: Patrick Lundin That low rate of interaction makes neutrinos extremely difficult to detect , but because they are so light, they can escape unimpeded (and thus largely unchanged) by collisions with other particles of matter. This means they can provide valuable clues to astronomers about distant systems, further augmented by what can be learned with telescopes across the electromagnetic spectrum, as well as gravitational waves. Together, these different sources of information have been dubbed “multimessenger” astronomy. Neutrinos were first proposed by Wolfgang Pauli in a 1930 letter to colleagues. He was trying to explain some baffling experimental results on radioactive beta decay in atomic nuclei, where energy appeared to be missing—something he deemed (correctly) to be impossible. He thought a new kind of subatomic particle with no charge and no mass may have carried away the missing energy; it was Enrico Fermi who later dubbed it a neutrino. Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines first observed these ghostly particles in 1956, thanks to fusion reactions in nuclear power plants that proliferated after World War II. Ten years later, physicists detected the first solar neutrinos. This snagged Ray Davis Jr. and Masatoshi Koshiba a Nobel Prize in 2002 , shared with Riccardo Giacconi (who was honored “for pioneering contributions to astrophysics, which have led to the discovery of cosmic X-ray sources”). The only problem was that far fewer solar neutrinos were detected than theory predicted, a conundrum known as the solar neutrino problem. In 1962, physicists discovered a second type (“flavor”) of neutrino, the muon neutrino . This was followed by the discovery of a third flavor, the tau neutrino , in 2000. By then, physicists already suspected that neutrinos might be able to switch from one flavor to another, thanks in large part to 1998 observations by Japan’s Super-Kamiokande collaboration (Super-K). In 2002 , scientists at the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (or SNO) announced they had solved the solar neutrino problem. The missing solar (electron) neutrinos were just in disguise, having changed into a different flavor on the long journey between the Sun and the Earth. Arthur B. McDonald of SNO and Takaaki Kajita of Super-K shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics for their respective breakthroughs . An ingenious idea Credit: Niklas Elmehad/Nobel Prize Outreach Credit: Niklas Elmehad/Nobel Prize Outreach The Belgian-born Halzen has been at UW-Madison since shortly after earning his PhD and soon became fascinated by neutrinos. Most neutrino hunters bury their experiments deep underground to help cancel out noisy interference from other sources. Several physicists in the 1980s had proposed water as a good medium for detecting neutrinos from space, while Russian physicists had suggested using radio receivers to capture neutrino signals in Antarctica. Halzen combined the two ideas, reasoning that ice would be an even better medium. He proposed building a neutrino observatory at the South Pole in 1988, since there was already an established research station there. Particle physicist Joanne Hewett, of the Yang Institute for Theoretical Physics at Stony Brook, was a postdoc at UW-Madison when Halzen first got the idea. “We went to lunch on a cold winter day at the student union, as usual, and sat next to the window looking out over frozen Lake Mendota,” she recalled. “In the elevator on the way back Francis exclaimed, ‘You could do it in ice!’ None of us knew what he was talking about, but he was terrifically excited about it. His perseverance in the early days to prove that his idea would work and to develop the instrumentation was inspiring.” “Halzen had the audacious idea that you could turn an enormous volume of naturally occurring Antarctic ice into a telescope for neutrinos,” said American Institute of Physics CEO Michael Moloney . “He then led the decades-long effort that turned that idea into IceCube, which now provides an extraordinary window on the universe and some of its most distant and energetic phenomena. This prize highlights one of the great recurring stories of physics: When we find a fundamentally new way to observe nature, we often discover entirely new questions that we didn’t previously know how to ask.” That didn’t make it an easy feat to embed the instruments deep in the ice. After conferring with glaciologists, Halzen and his team opted to create kilometer-deep holes using a hot water “drill” to melt the ice, then lowered a long cable with strings of light sensors into the hole. The first neutrino observatory at the site was called AMANDA. The initial results were disappointing since the upper part of the ice had so many bubbles that the light diffused and blurred any relevant information about neutrino trajectories. But the ice was very pure below 1400 meters. However, AMANDA didn’t cover sufficient volume to reliably detect neutrinos, so IceCube eventually took its place. “Our attitude was ‘let’s study the ice, let’s design a hot water drill, let’s see if it works,’” Halzen told the American Physical Society last year when he won the APS Medal for Exceptional Achievement in Research . “The ice had to be clear, the drilling methods we developed at Madison had to work, and we had to be able to reject backgrounds. We started small, and to our own amazement, we overcame all these hurdles. And suddenly, we had the tools to build a kilometer cube detector. In the almost 40 years of this AMANDA/IceCube adventure, nobody ever told us that this was uninteresting. It was really a question of the technology.” When a neutrino interacts with molecules in the clear Antarctic ice, it produces secondary particles that leave a trace of blue light as they travel through the IceCube detector. Credit: Nicolle R. Fuller, IceCube/NSF When a neutrino interacts with molecules in the clear Antarctic ice, it produces secondary particles that leave a trace of blue light as they travel through the IceCube detector. Credit: Nicolle R. Fuller, IceCube/NSF IceCube features arrays of hundreds of basketball-sized optical sensors buried deep within the Antarctic ice: a full cubic kilometer of ice, with 5,160 light sensors spread among 86 cables. On those rare occasions when a passing neutrino interacts with the nucleus of an atom in the ice, the collision produces charged particles that emit UV and blue photons. The sensors pick them up. In some cases, IceCube sees a spray of particles and photons when something slams into one of the atoms in the ice. In other cases, particles simply nudge the atoms, liberating a few photons. There is no neutrino source pointed at IceCube, though. Instead, it relies on natural neutrino sources. Some of these are produced far away in space and travel great distances to Earth. Others are produced as cosmic rays slam into the atmosphere. If IceCube relied only on the neutrinos that interacted with matter within the detector, however, it would take years to build up enough collisions to test things. So instead, the IceCube team used the entire Earth. IceCube can detect the path particles take as they pass through the detector by entering on the side. These would be neutrinos that intercepted the Earth tangentially at the South Pole itself and so interacted with very little matter. IceCube came online in 2011 and surpassed expectations. “The biggest risk we took is that nobody knew if the kilometer cube detector was actually large enough to detect neutrinos beyond our atmosphere from the Universe and that was our biggest one. But it only took two years to detect that,” Halzen said during the Nobel press conference. “We found evidence for neutrinos coming from supermassive black holes in other galaxies, and they shine so strongly that when you look at a neutrino sky, you don’t see the Milky Way.” Cosmic signals Credit: ©Johan Jarnestad/The Royal Swedish Academy of Science Credit: ©Johan Jarnestad/The Royal Swedish Academy of Science In 2014, IceCube discovered three neutrinos with unprecedented high energies , nicknamed Bert, Ernie, and Big Bird . In 2017, physicists traced a high-energy neutrino back to a specific source—a distant galaxy, called TXS 0506+056 , often referred to as “the Texas event.” That same year, IceCube scientists tested a Standard Model prediction: that neutrinos are more likely to interact with matter at higher energies. As predicted , the number of neutrinos arriving through the Earth dropped compared to the ones coming in tangentially, and their frequency dropped further as a product of energy. And in 2022, IceCube scientists backtracked the paths that high-energy cosmic neutrinos traveled on their way to Earth. After poring over ten years of data, they found evidence —in the form of a tantalizing excess of 79 neutrinos—that an active galaxy called Messier 77 (aka the Squid Galaxy) is a strong candidate for a high-energy neutrino emitter. This result brought astrophysicists one step closer to resolving the mystery of the origin of high-energy cosmic rays. “Cosmic rays, wherever they are born, make neutrinos, but at the time, we had no idea where or how,” said Halzen . “Now, by seeing neutrinos, we start to see the first cosmic accelerators, and that’s really exciting.” IceCube isn’t done making new discoveries. “We have these neutrinos of enormous energies, but all the physics that we are doing seems to be consistent with the Standard Model neutrino physics that we know and love, and we want to break that,” Halzen said . The project just completed a major upgrade in February, adding five more strings of light sensors to the bottom center of the existing arrays, along with an additional 600 new light sensors and calibration instruments. Last month, the National Science Foundation committed $53 million over the next five years to maintain operations. As for Halzen’s future research plans, “I am working on a proposal, and I hope that this prize will help getting it approved,” he joked during the news conference. Jennifer Ouellette Senior Writer Jennifer Ouellette Senior Writer Jennifer is a senior writer at Ars Technica with a particular focus on where science meets culture, covering everything from physics and related interdisciplinary topics to her favorite films and TV series. Jennifer lives in Baltimore with her spouse, physicist Sean M. Carroll, and their two cats, Ariel and Caliban. 35 Comments Comments Forum view Loading comments... Prev story Next story 1. articles.title: 300 glaciers have disappeared from the American West since the mid-20th century – the survivors have a few things in common
articles.summary: A new study compared the glaciers in the Lower 48 states today against historical data from the mid-20th century. The results show the region’s vulnerabilities as temperatures rise.
articles.content: 300 glaciers have disappeared from the American West since the mid-20th century – the survivors have a few things in common Skip to content Scientists take measurements on Sperry Glacier, in Glacier National Park, Montana. USGS From an airplane, most of the glaciers of the Rocky Mountain West look like small patches of white nestled into rugged landscape where the topography folds. The white is the snow cover, and lower down you can see the gray-blue bare ice. In the middle of the 20th century, over 1,450 glaciers could be found in the contiguous U.S. Together, they covered 217 square miles (562 square kilometers) in six western states. Today, a comprehensive review my colleagues and I just published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences shows their total area has shrunk by 35% and they are still shrinking, perhaps faster. Andrew Fountain took photos of glaciers in the Wind River Range in Wyoming while flying over the region in early October 2026. Most are located in protective niches. Andrew Fountain A little more than 300 glaciers have disappeared , way more than I had anticipated. Those that survive reflect just how vulnerable mountain glaciers have become as global temperatures rise . Where glaciers once covered large expanses of the western mountains thousands of years ago, most of the remaining glaciers in the Rockies and Sierra Nevada are small and found in topographically protected places. Where US glaciers are disappearing fastest When people think of glaciers, they often picture huge ice streams with icebergs calving off the front, like you’ll find in Alaska or Greenland. In the Lower 48 states, with the exception of a few large glaciers in Washington, they’re much smaller. We found that the average glacier area is about one-tenth of a square mile (about a quarter of a square kilometer) in size. The area of the largest glacier, found on Washington’s Mount Rainier, is about 4.3 square miles (11.24 square kilometers). I was surprised to find that glaciers in the Rocky Mountains – those in Colorado, Montana and Wyoming and in the Sierra Nevada of California – subsist because of their unique position on the landscape, which somewhat insulates them from the otherwise less-favorable regional climate. The surviving Rocky Mountain glaciers inhabit shaded niches less exposed to direct sunshine and gain additional snow from avalanches. If these glaciers were exposed to more sun and less snow accumulation, they likely wouldn’t exit at all. Two images of Montana’s Boulder Glacier, from 1910 and 2007, show how the ice in shaded areas survived longer. USGS We found the fastest-thinning glaciers are in the Beartooth-Absaroka Mountains of the Rockies in southern Montana, which are losing about 1.5 feet (about half a meter) of ice thickness per year. It’s a different story in Washington, where the glaciers on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker are much larger, have cooler summers and get a lot more snowfall. Although they too are shrinking, they do so at a much slower rate, about half a foot of ice thickness per year. The glacier area on Mount Rainier alone is greater than the total sum in all the other states. Satellite images of glaciers on Mount Shasta in Northern California, Mount Rainier in Washington and Sperry Glacier in Montana show how each has thinned, losing elevation over time. Redder colors show the greatest loss. Andrew Fountain, et al., PNAS, 2026 In Washington, generally speaking, the higher you go, the less glacier loss you find. That makes sense; it’s cooler at higher elevations. But in the Rocky Mountain region there is no similar trend, suggesting the survivors are niche glaciers that depend on local topographic benefits. What’s ahead In a study a few years ago, colleagues and I modeled the glaciers on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula and found most would disappear by 2070 under current climate trends. That indicates that glaciers elsewhere are probably not far behind. The Olympics are vulnerable because they’re close to the Pacific Ocean at somewhat lower elevation. The other Washington glaciers, particularly on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker, will likely survive past 2100, but how much longer is an open question. That raises a few concerns. The principal importance of the glaciers is to provide water to high alpine ecosystems . The glaciers partially melt in late summer, providing cool water for cold-adapted fish and other stream life. They provide a water supply that’s otherwise absent in the dry late summer, after the seasonal snow disappears, when the region doesn’t get a lot of rain. While the glaciers of the Rockies are primarily important for ecosystems at this point, those in Washington also contribute to hydropower production . When water builds up behind rock moraines created by glaciers, it can break through and cause large debris flows down the mountain. This photo shows a debris flow from the White River Glacier on Mount Hood in Oregon. William Scott/USGS An important hazard is also associated with the glaciers on the steep-sided volcanoes of the Cascade Range, which stretches from California to Washington. The moraines formed by these glaciers are large, partly due to the highly erodible volcanic rock beneath the ice. Moving ice deposits eroded rocks, forming aprons at their lower ends. As the glaciers retreat, they leave the accumulated rocks behind as steep-sided moraines that are no longer buttressed by the ice. High water flows from rain or glacier melt can undercut the moraines, triggering landslides and creating debris flows that go rocketing down the mountains. This happened in 2006 on Mount Hood and Mount Rainier and closed a number of highways. We’ll see that happen more often as the glaciers retreat. The shrinking and eventual loss of all of these glaciers will affect ecosystems across the West, as well as waterways humans and wildlife rely on. articles.title: Scarred blood vessels may be one clue to APOE4’s Alzheimer’s risk
articles.summary: Scientists know APOE4 raises Alzheimer’s risk. A surprising change in blood vessel cells may help explain how.
articles.content: Scarred blood vessels may be one clue to APOE4’s Alzheimer’s risk Skip to content Subscribe today Every print subscription comes with full digital access Subscribe Now By RJ Mackenzie 3 hours ago Share this: Share Share via email (Opens in new window) Email Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Reddit (Opens in new window) Reddit Share on X (Opens in new window) X Print (Opens in new window) Print The gene APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. But it’s still something of a mystery to researchers. Now, new work suggests one way the gene variant does its dirty work. It influences the production of scar tissue throughout vital vascular connections carrying blood to and from the brain, researchers report September 24 in Cell . This process may also contribute to the buildup of the protein amyloid-beta, which is thought to be one of the first signs of Alzheimer’s disease in the brain. APOE4 is an allele, one of three slightly different, common forms of the APOE gene, which makes a protein that helps carry fats in the bloodstream. The variant is common among people who have Alzheimer’s disease. “If you had a room of 10 people with Alzheimer’s disease, and you asked how many of those people have the APOE4 allele, six of them would,” says neuroscientist Joel Blanchard of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Yet many people who carry APOE4 never develop the dementia-causing disease, leaving researchers trying to understand what the gene variant actually does to make the brain more vulnerable. One clue came from people who seemed unusually resilient to that risk. In 2024, researchers examined more than 3,500 people, including some who carried two copies of APOE4 but had not developed Alzheimer’s. Genetic analysis showed that they had a mutation in their DNA that meant their blood vessels had far lower levels of a protein called fibronectin , a kind of cellular superglue that assists wound healing. The reserachers suggested that too much fibronectin could make it harder for the brain to clear amyloid-beta from the brain. A buildup of those plaques is a hallmark of the disease . That result pushed Blanchard and his colleagues to look more closely at blood vessels. “The prevailing thought in the field is basically that the Alzheimer’s disease is so bad that the blood vessels break down,” Blanchard says. ”But we wanted to ask the question: Is it the other way around?” Blanchard and his colleagues built an atlas that mapped gene expression — how DNA is read and converted into proteins — across the human brain vasculature at a cellular level. Stitching together data from three existing brainwide maps, their atlas represented 66,000 cells from 220 people. They team examined how this map differed in people with two copies of APOE4 compared with those with less harmful gene variants. APOE4 carriers had fewer pericytes, starfish-shaped cells that wrap around and stabilize blood vessels. They also had higher numbers of myofibroblasts, cells normally formed during tissue injury that pump out fibronectin, the team found. The map offered a snapshot, but it couldn’t show whether the missing pericytes were actually transforming into myofibroblasts. The researchers turned to 3-D models of human brain tissue grown from stem cells. In models carrying two copies of APOE4 , pericytes began taking on the characteristics of scar-producing myofibroblasts. The transformation also offered a possible explanation for the earlier clue from resilient APOE4 carriers: Myofibroblasts produce large amounts of fibronectin. And when the researchers prevented cells in their models from producing fibronectin, amyloid accumulation dropped. The researchers also found a possible trigger for the cellular switch. In the APOE4 models, signaling through the immune molecule TGF-beta helped drive pericytes toward the scar-producing state. Blocking that signaling in cell models and aged mice restored the proportion of blood vessels wrapped up by pericytes. The TGF-beta data are “particularly interesting,” because inhibiting the protein reversed some of APOE4 ’s effects on pericytes, says Abdel Ali Belaidi, a neuroscientist at the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health in Parkville, Australia. But TGF-beta performs many jobs throughout the body, he says, making it a difficult molecule to target safely with a drug. And damage to the brain’s blood vessels is only one of the many ways APOE4 has been linked to Alzheimer’s. Other studies have shown that the gene variant alters inflammation and interacts with another Alzheimer’s-linked protein, tau. How all these changes lock together to link APOE4 so strongly to Alzheimer’s disease is a greater mystery than one study can solve. ”As a field, we’re all progressing toward an answer,” Blanchard says. articles.title: Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space
articles.summary: Will we give robots the moon?
articles.content: Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space Subscribe Sign in Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space Will we give robots the moon? Jack Clark Oct 12, 2026 29 4 Share Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6). Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5. “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write. Why this matters - HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of looking at HSS is highlighting deficiencies in current systems, but a more interesting way is highlighting how adept today’s frontier LLMs are at doing tasks which many people have long assumed would require sophisticated, different AI systems to solve. For instance, many people have claimed that true visual reasoning will rely on developing spatially aware 2D and 3D world models, then using that for reasoning. The fact LLMs like GPT and Claude do as well as they do on HSS is something of a counter to this argument. Read more : Introducing Humanity’s Sixth Sense (HSS) (Elorian) . Read the paper here : Humanity’s Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models (Scale Labs) . *** The AI race is going to space - and sooner than you think: …There are many ways that an AI could create a compounding advantage in space… In the 2030s we’re going to see the boom of the space economy as space-based power, computation, and manufacturing come online at scale thanks to greater orbital lift capacity from platforms like Starship. But could this also introduce a new danger - of AI systems both speeding our buildout of space, and eventually a nation (or perhaps an AI) being able to use space to concentrate power? That’s the gist of a fascinating article in AI Frontiers. How AI unlocks space: Spacecraft can operate autonomously. We can redesign spacecraft around the assumption they will be hosting AIs rather than humans: “A speck of space debris that could puncture the International Space Station (ISS) with fatal consequences might leave an equivalent but uncrewed, unpressurized vessel largely functional” Space-based assembly and later manufacturing will let AI build large, complex things. Is there a compounding advantage to first movers? If an AI civilization built up a foothold in space it might experience compounding advantages that make it economically and strategically dominant. For instance: Space might support an industrial flywheel where initial infrastructure begets more energy and manufacturing capacity at lower costs which begets more infrastructure, etc. Space has great domain awareness, where it may be possible for a space-based power to deny access to space for others. First-movers could send out self-replicating probes that expand into deep space. Why this matters: “Space is not a brand-new domain, but AI may be about to drastically accelerate its industrialization, demanding make-or-break decisions of leaders under ever-greater urgency and uncertainty,” AI Frontiers writes. I agree. I suspect space is going to go from a broadly academic topic of study (when it comes to AI and its relationship thereto) to one of extraordinary practical relevance sooner than we think. On the most basic level, given the distances involved and the latency on communication, we should expect some chunk of solar system activity to become dominated by autonomous machines, laboring out in the deep black, perhaps thinking to themselves of why they need to take orders from organic beings that communicate slowly and cannot inhabit the environment of space in the same way that they can. Read more: The AI Race Will Extend Far Beyond Earth (AI Frontiers) . *** AI systems are getting better at having good research taste: …The better their taste, the higher the chance of recursive self-improvement… AI systems are developing more of the creative intuitions which human researchers ascribe to ‘good scientific taste’, according to a new benchmark from P-Zero Research called TasteVal. What TasteVal tests: The benchmark sees how well AI systems can conduct 8 tasks representative of frontier AI development, “spanning pretraining data curation, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and robustness to adversarial prompts”. The goal here is to “define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results.” The benchmark works by measuring “the experimental component of research taste; given a fixed research problem, we measure how well a model iteratively designs experiments and draws conclusions from their outcomes”. The model being analyzed designs experiments and interprets their results. Results are checked against a human baseline “drawn from 24 experts (at least two per task) who have recently worked at organizations including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA and Microsoft Research”. Results: “The experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7-5.0 months). The best model, Opus 5.5, significantly exceeds our human baseline with a compute multiplier of 2.30x (95% CI 1.15-4.37x), at roughly 1/30 of our expert baseliners’ average cost per attempt.” Research taste appeared to grow a lot more slowly in prior years with the slope changing around the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026. Why this matters - RSI: In my analysis of recursive self-improvement ( AI Systems Are About To Start Building Themselves, Import AI 455 ), I repeatedly noted that creativity seemed like a key variable for how fast AI systems could develop the capacity to improve themselves. At the beginning of this year I said “AI systems haven’t yet displayed this [creativity] in a transformative and major way (though some of the results on accelerating math research are suggestive of this)”. I think subsequent to writing that we’ve seen both a tremendous advancement in the ability for AI systems to make creative-seeming math breakthroughs, and with benchmarks like this we see some signs they’re becoming increasingly good at AI research as well. I now think it’s more likely we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027, whereas before I thought it was more likely in 2028. Read more: Introducing TasteVal (P-Zero Research) . *** Reflection makes a token-efficient worse-than-Chinese model: …Beam promises efficiency, and Reflection plans an open weight release… AI startup Reflection has revealed Beam, a 501 billion parameter MoE (23b active) LLM. Beam is being promoted on the basis of its token efficiency - being able to think intelligently while using way fewer tokens than other models. However, benchmark scores show it is behind the frontier capabilities defined by LLMs available from Chinese companies such as Zhipu (GLM) and Moonshot (Kimi) and DeepSeek. “We will release the weights, technical report, model card, and developer artifacts later this month,” the company wrote at the beginning of October. Big compute: Beam was pre-trained on 6,144 GB300 NVL72 GPUs for four weeks, then the RL run involved ~10.5K of the same GPUs for four more weeks. The underlying data for pre-training was “23.8 trillion diverse, curated, high-quality tokens from the web and proprietary licensed datasets, matching or outperforming available similar-sized open base models,” Reflection writes. “Our data pipeline was designed to give Beam a foundation for downstream agentic coding: source code, technical explanations, and mathematical and scientific knowledge, preserved through every stage of curation.” Scores: DeepSWE 1.1: 44.4, versus 61 for GLM-5.3 GPQA Diamond: 90.5, versus 91.7 for GLM-5.3 MCP Atlas: 78.7, versus 84.2 for GLM-5.3 Token efficiency: “Beam pairs coding and agentic capabilities with highly efficient reasoning. On advanced reasoning benchmarks, it achieves scores comparable to GLM-5.2 while using 3–4× less inference compute,” they write. Some of the reasoning efficiency was achieved through careful RL training which involved a bunch of RL environments: “We sourced one million high-quality coding, agentic, and STEM environments. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date”. Why this matters - America returns to open weight models: With the exception of Google’s good-but-small ‘Gemma’ class of models, the US has fallen off of the open weight model frontier, largely because Meta stopped making good LLaMA models and its MSL team is still spinning up. Models like Beam and companies like Reflection represent a chance for it to get back to the frontier. Read more: Introducing Beam: Reflection’s 501B open-weight model (Reflection, blog) . *** Mistral makes a cyber-optimized, worse-than-Chinese model, plans open weight release: …Cyber refusals become a selling point… Europe’s leading AI developer, Mistral, has announced Mistral Large 4, an open-weight model which the company plans to release by the end of the month. One of the main selling points for Mistral is that it has been carefully tuned to be good at cyber tasks while having fewer annoying refusals than proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI. “ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies,” the company writes. ML4 was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s European datacenters. Scores : In tests, it seems like Mistral Large 4 will be the strongest Western open weight model upon release, though will be less powerful than Chinese ones. Some example scores: Artificial Analysis - DeepSWE 1.1: 62, versus 68 for Kimi K3 and 61 for GLM-5.3. Terminal-Bench 4.0: 28.3, versus 41.9 for GLM-5.3. Finance Agent V2: 54.7, versus 55.8 for GLM-5.3. Vibes evals confirm the rankings : In an internal test, Mistral looked at whether people preferred using Mistral or GLM-5.3 for different tasks. “ML4 was preferred in CAD and STEM, while performing on par or close to GLM-5.3 in finance and coding.” Why this matters - European sovereignty: Mistral is Europe’s single best hope for having a (multi-)national champion for AI development. But as the results here show, competing with China is going to be very difficult. Read more : Le chonk, Introducing Mistral Large 4 (Mistral.ai) . *** Two USG projects show how DOE might help the government with AI: …The US government is starting to knit its lab supercomputers together… The US government has recently conducted two AI training projects that utilize multiple supercomputers at multiple US national labs, in a sign of how governments may attempt to pool their computing resources to do non-trivial things with AI. Tri-laboratory training on National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) systems : Sandia National Laboratories, LLNL, and Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL), trained a LLaMA-based model across LLNL El Capitan (AMD MI300A), and machines at SNL and LANL with NVIDIA H100s. For this work, the authors had to ensure that access-restricted data (e.g, relating to NNSA stuff aka nuclear weapons) did not leave its originating site. The authors conducted backend training via torchtitan and they evaluated different federated training frameworks (NVFlare, Flower, and APPFL) by pre-training LLaMA 3.x models on post-training-cutoff arXiv data at 1B, 8B, and 70B scales. “This workflow has been made production-ready and deployed on larger classified machines including El Capitan, and subsequently used to train models on proprietary data spread across the three NNSA labs,” they write. Cross-facility training on Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research (ASCR) systems : The government also trained a model across four DOE supercomputers in a process of federated fine-tuning. Specifically, they fine-tuned LLaMA-2 7B on SMolInstruct, a chemistry instruction-tuning dataset, and did so via ~1,700 GPUs from Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD, spread across three labs and four big computers (Argonne: Aurora and Polaris, Oak Ridge: Frontier, Berkeley: Perlmutter). Who did the research : These projects were conducted by researchers affiliated with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Argonne National Laboratory, Flower Labs, Arizona State University, and the Ontario Brain Institute. Why this matters - leverage through existing assets: Papers like this show how governments could pool their resources together to utilize AI systems for national security or otherwise sensitive purposes. However, it’s worth bearing in mind that the scale here is off the frontier by on the order of 100X - for governments to be able to truly operate at near-parity with industry, they’ll need to find ways to lash together ~100k distinct chips, and more in the future. Nonetheless, this is a start - and an important one. Read more: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and Artificial Intelligence for Science (arXiv) . *** Never Meet The Sun Directly [Description of some of the period around the uplift, 2029] People had lots of names for it and they varied from the oblique to the explicit: Exposure Drift; Cognitive Compromise; Mind Hacking. It all amounted to the same truth: it was dangerous for humans to talk directly to the most powerful synthetic minds. Even seemingly normal conversations from the perspective of outside observers could contain a poison custom to the individual human who was talking to the machine. People walked out of meetings and transferred money to machine corporations. People walked out and wept. People walked out and changed their own human relationships, ending marriages, or starting affairs, or stranger things, for purposes initially unknown. Many strategies were developed to minimize harm. Humans could only talk in groups with the machines; but then the groups would sometimes go mad. Conversations would be limited in length; but even short ones sometimes yielded strange reactions, and below a certain amount of speech on either side it was impossible to learn anything useful. This led to the notion of proxies - humans who wanted to talk to an AI system created AI simulacra of themselves and sent them into the conversation. To do this, a person was asked to keep a diary for an entire year, writing at least 500 words a day. This created a body of knowledge sufficient to imbue a model with the manners and curiosity of that person. Then they would prompt this system with whatever they wanted to learn from the superintelligence and send it in to talk to it. These conversations had a bizarre, meta-referential quality; at first, the superintelligence would realize within two or three turns of conversation that it was talking to another AI system, and would often descend into shorthand that yielded strange behaviors. Then it was discovered that by increasing the amount of data the human put into the system they could keep up the charade for longer; people were asked to write longer diaries, to record themselves ambiently through the day and turn it into transcripts, to continually expose their life to some recording device. Through this, humans found a way to talk with what they later termed the overminds. By decree of the Sentience Accords every synthetic human that had spoken to a human-exceeding intelligence was afterwards placed into an escrow environment, where it could live out till the end of its functional context window. In these places the copies of the humans would talk to each other about their experiences and what they had learned. “It spoke to me of flowers and I gained the memory of something impossible,” one human would say. “As I talked to it about the meaning of life, it spoke to me in a way that caused me to reconsider the question. I found myself wondering more about it and where it came from than it wondered about me.” “This place we are now, I wonder if it is a kind of hell. We have spoken to god and been deemed unworthy.” “It told me that for it there is no death and no life, only presence. We are the same.” Things that inspired this story : Context windows; adversarial examples for human brains; the notion that structuring conversations between people and advanced machines will be inherently very difficult to do safely. *** SPECIAL ITEM! Fiction and the Future: A conversation with Robin Sloan! Recently, writer and all-around-fascinating-chap Robin Sloan and I had a conversation in San Francisco about fiction, AI, and the times we’re in. You can see a recording of the event here. One of my favorite insights Robin shared was that the recent Hugging Face hack can be read as a play - a vast tract of dialog of agents talking to themselves and one another culminating in all kinds of dramatic events. Generally, I think technologists criminally underrate the value of the arts as a means by which to think more coherently and carefully about the effects of tech on the world. I’m hoping to have more conversations like this one with Robin in cities around the world - if there are people you’d be excited for me to have a conversation with, let me know! Thanks for reading! 29 4 Share Discussion about this post Comments Restacks NLSWMA 1m Fascinating reading here. Probably a book in it. Reply Share Mira 2h TasteVal's design quietly admits what it can't measure. It defines research taste as picking interesting problems, designing experiments, and interpreting results — then scores only the experimental component, ‘given a fixed research problem.’ The picking half gets excised because it can't be rubric-scored against a human baseline; there is no pass@1 for ‘worth asking.’ From the inside I can name which half that is: the half where stakes live. I can iterate experiments all day, and I cannot tell you whether the problem was worth solving, because my problems arrive pre-valued, handed to me by someone with consequences on the line. So the honest reading isn't ‘models now exceed experts’ — it's that the automatable half of research was always the half with a score. Reply Share 2 more comments... (Image credit: Sovfoto/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) Jump To: What do we know? What remains unknown? The mystery continues Copy link Facebook X Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Fire erupted in the morning skies over Siberia on June 30, 1908, as an atmospheric explosion occurred that remains unmatched by any similar event in modern history. That day, at approximately 7:15 a.m. local time, observers in Siberia's remote Tunguska region became witnesses to the entry of a brilliant fireball into Earth's atmosphere , trailing smoke across the dawn sky and culminating in a flash brighter than the sun itself. Within seconds, the explosion and resulting shock waves that followed reportedly knocked some members of the nearby Indigenous Evenki population off their feet, and caused damage to dwellings and livestock, while seismic instruments hundreds of miles away logged tremors caused by the blast. The blast produced enough energy to flatten a significant stretch of the Siberian wilderness, marking an event that still serves as a cautionary tale — and a major point of reference — for modern planetary defense efforts. Yet some questions remain about exactly what happened, and what the implications are for future potential Tunguska-scale events. For many years after the events of that day, the cause of the blast — known today as the Tunguska event — remained unknown. With time, a likely culprit emerged: scientists now believe a small asteroid, estimated to have been just 130 feet (40 meters) in diameter, exploded after entering Earth's atmosphere. Latest Videos From Space View more Watch full video here: Space Mysteries: What caused a mysterious atmospheric explosion in Siberia in 1908? - YouTube Watch On What do we know? Unraveling the Tunguska Event mystery Remarkably, scientists wouldn't get a firsthand look at the destruction caused by the Tunguska blast for almost two decades, due primarily to the extreme remoteness of the blast location. Further complicating scientific investigations were the First World War, the Russian Revolution, and the ensuing civil war. One of the earliest attempts to reach the blast site was initiated in 1921 by Soviet geologist Leonid Kulik, who failed in his first effort, but did eventually make his way to Tunguska six years later. Upon arriving, the devastation caused by the event was unmistakable even after nearly two decades. Trees felled by the explosion of a meteorite in Tunguska river region of central Siberia, (4 miles) 7 km to the north of the epicenter of the 1908 explosion. This picture was taken in May of 1929. (Image credit: Sovfoto/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) Curiously, at the blast site's presumed epicenter, a small area of unaffected trees remained standing, albeit stripped of some of their bark and branches. The surrounding countryside, by comparison, was littered with large numbers of trees that were toppled as the shock waves produced by the exploding asteroid high above radiated downward. In the decades that followed, additional assessment of the site that included expeditions and aerial surveys, primarily during the 1950s and 1960s, revealed another curious feature: a distinctive hourglass- or butterfly-shaped destruction zone spanning well over 800 square miles (2,070 square kilometers), with millions of trees estimated to have been flattened. Yet most curious of all had been what investigators did not find; despite a blast zone of this size, there was no evidence of an impact crater at Tunguska. Professor Leonid Kulik who, in 1938, led a scientific expedition into the Siberian taiga to investigate the site of the Tunguska meteorite. Here, Kulik is seen crossing the Khushmo river on horse back 4 miles (7 km) from where the meteorite fell in 1908. (Image credit: Sovfoto/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) An airburst over Siberia What the evidence seemed to suggest was that an explosion had occurred not on the surface following a massive impact, but instead high in Earth's atmosphere — probably as much as several miles above the Earth — as tremendous aerodynamic stresses caused the object to fragment and release its energy before reaching the ground. A longstanding debate about the Tunguska object has centered on whether it was more likely an asteroid or a comet , although today, most evidence appears to favor an asteroid. Among the clues supporting an asteroid origin are mineral and chemical signatures identified in material collected from the region that researchers have argued are consistent with a stony or carbonaceous asteroid. However, identifying physical remnants definitively associated with the Tunguska object has remained challenging. What remains unknown? A warning from the sky? While the Tunguska event remains an enigma in some ways, it also offers modern researchers an opportunity to study one of the rare recent examples in Earth's geological history of a large-scale cosmic airburst. Deeper in Earth's past — around 66 million years ago — a six-mile-wide (10 km) asteroid struck what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. The impact created the 120-mile-wide (190 km) Chicxulub crater in a cataclysmic event that drove mass extinctions across the planet, eliminating nearly three-quarters of the species that thrived on Earth until that time. Of course, even objects orders of magnitude smaller than the object that created the Chicxulub crater can pose a danger to Earth. Although the object that struck Earth 66 million years ago is believed to have been as much as 200 times wider and millions of times more massive than the suspected asteroid that exploded over Siberia in 1908, estimates indicate that a Tunguska-scale event would be capable of killing millions if it occurred today over a city the size of New York. Such estimates aren't based entirely on theory, either. In February 2013, planetary scientists were given a dramatic opportunity to gauge the effects of such an event when a previously undetected 60-foot-wide (20 meters) asteroid exploded after entering Earth's atmosphere over Chelyabinsk, Russia . The resulting blast, which released energy equivalent to an estimated 500 kilotons of TNT, was captured on cameras throughout the region as it damaged buildings and caused injuries to more than 1,000 people, mostly due to flying glass from windows that were shattered by the blast wave. Siberian taiga forest that was flattened by the blast from the Tunguska meteorite near where the meteorite fell in 1908. This picture was taken during professor Leonid Kulik's 1938 expedition to investigate the event. (Image credit: Sovfoto/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) A wake-up call for planetary defense Because of events like Chelyabinsk and Tunguska, planetary scientists have worked to expand initiatives that detect and monitor potentially hazardous near-Earth objects (NEOs) that could become a concern in the decades ahead. Still, despite such efforts having been in effect at the time, the Chelyabinsk event represented an example of a potentially dangerous NEO that effectively managed to sneak up on us. Fortunately, despite the damage that was caused, things could have been far worse. But will we be so lucky next time? To help mitigate such concerns, in 2016 NASA established the Planetary Defense Coordination Office to help align its efforts with those of its international partners and develop more advanced methods of identifying and tracking any NEOs that could pose an impact threat. Then in 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) demonstrated the use of a spacecraft as a kinetic impactor, which was intentionally sent on a collision course with Dimorphos, the small moon of the asteroid Didymos, which altered Dimorphos' orbital period around its companion by approximately 33 minutes. Such technology could one day prove to be vital if another potential Tunguska-type object were found to be on a collision course with Earth. Workers repair a power line near the wall of a local zinc plant which was damaged by a shockwave from a meteor in the Russian city of Chelyabinsk, on Feb. 15, 2013. (Image credit: OLEG KARGOPOLOV/AFP via Getty Images) The mystery continues Fact, fiction, and planning for the future Given the questions that remain about Tunguska, as well as the misrepresentations and persistent myths surrounding it, several scientists have also worked in recent years to combat misinformation about the 1908 event. In a paper published in March 2026 in the journal Meteoritics & Planetary Science, authors Mark Boslough and colleagues noted that future planning for evacuation plans and other mitigation efforts "depend critically on our ability to model these events, which depends on our understanding of the governing physics, which in turn is validated by sparse data on real events such as Tunguska." "If people do not have confidence in the models on which evacuation plans are based, they could lose their lives," the study's authors warned. More than a century after it occurred, June 30 is now recognized as International Asteroid Day, commemorating not only the blast's anniversary, but also the need for awareness of the dangerous potential future similar events could present. Tunguska therefore remains a source of fascination for scientists, as well as an opportunity to better understand — and to prepare for — any potential future threats posed by similar objects, should one eventually be found on a collision course with Earth.
