Close Caption : Artist's impression of ZTF J0440+2325, a brown dwarf (right) and a red dwarf (left) that orbit each other every 86.65 minutes. The brown dwarf overflows onto its companion, and the stream of material strikes the surface of the red dwarf, heating a large hot spot at the point of impact. Credits : Credit: Aaron Householder (MIT) Previous image Next image Like Earth, most planetary bodies circle their star in stable, detached orbits. These companionable systems can suddenly change when a planet comes too close to its star. In such a close encounter, a star can pull the planet in and swallow it whole. Across the galaxy, astronomers have seen plenty of stable, detached planetary systems. They have also observed a handful of stars quickly engulfing their planet. Now, for the first time, scientists have spotted a system that is striking a curious balance between the two extremes. And it’s revealing a new way that stars can interact with planetary companions. In a paper appearing today in Nature Astronomy , scientists at MIT and elsewhere have discovered a star leisurely snacking on a closely orbiting brown dwarf — a planet-like object that is more massive than a planet yet not quite as big as a star. The new system, named ZTF J0440+2325, is within the Milky Way galaxy, roughly 300 light years from Earth, and represents the first observation of a low-mass object that is slowly and steadily consuming material from another low-mass object. The rate at which the star is feeding from the brown dwarf suggests that this slow stellar cannibalism could carry on for hundreds of thousands, or even billions of years. “When we think of stars interacting with planets or brown dwarfs, the picture is always that the star eventually swallows the other thing,” says Kevin Burdge, assistant professor of physics at MIT. “This is what will happen to the Earth when the sun becomes a red giant. But here, we’ve found an alternative: Instead of swallowing the thing up, the star can gradually eat it, for billions of years.” The study’s MIT co-authors include Aaron Householder, Kaitlyn Shin, Saul Rappaport, Joheen Chakraborty, and Emma Chickles, along with collaborators from Caltech, the University of Hawaii, the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias and the Universidad de La Laguna in Spain, and the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics. A “weird triangle” The new system was spotted initially by the Zwicky Transient Facility. The ZTF uses a camera as part of a telescope at the Palomar Observatory, in California, to scan the sky for rapid changes in brightness, which could signal the presence of a supernova, a gamma-ray burst, or colliding neutron stars. Several years ago, Burdge was looking through ZTF data when he noticed a strange light curve, or pattern in brightness. Light curves for supernova resemble a bell curve, signaling the gradual brightening and then fading of a star as it bursts. But what Burdge picked out looked more like a triangle, that didn’t appear once, but again and again. “I remember first looking at this and thinking: Stars don’t make triangular waveforms like this,” he recalls. At the time, he and his colleagues were focused on a different signal, which they identified as a “black widow binary” — a system in which an extremely dense, spinning neutron star is slowly consuming a much smaller companion star, similar to how its arachnid namesake plays with its prey. Burdge wondered whether the triangle signal might also be from a black widow. But the light from the signal was puzzling. In black widow binaries, the light appears to wobble, as a result of a very light, low-mass object, such as a small companion star, whipping around a much heavier object, such as a neutron star. “We weren’t seeing that whipping back and forth here,” Burdge says. “It didn’t make any sense. We couldn’t explain what this was.” But they had a hunch: Could the signal be coming not from a wobbly, David-and-Goliath system, but from a more balanced pair of objects, each with a similarly low mass? “If you have less mass in the system overall, things can gently orbit each other without whipping back and forth,” Burdge says. “That was the idea. But we never had any proof. And this weird triangle just sat for years.” A slow and steady fireball Recently, Burdge and Householder, a graduate student in MIT’s Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, decided to revisit the triangle mystery. From the original ZTF signal, they determined the location of its source to be within the Milky Way galaxy, around 300 light years from Earth. They focused multiple telescopes on the source, named ZTF J0440+2325. From these observations, they measured various properties of the source, including its wobble. Compared to black widows and other similar binaries, the wobbling from ZTF J0440+2325 was much smaller — but not insignificant. “That was the real clincher for this system,” Householder says. “When we measured that wobble, we found we were not seeing a black widow. This was a low-mass star that’s orbited by a brown dwarf. The wobble was too small in amplitude to be anything else.” They determined that the star and the brown dwarf are extremely close, with the brown dwarf circling the star every 87 minutes, in an orbit that could fit within the diameter of the sun. Both objects are small by stellar standards. The star is around 85 times as massive as Jupiter, while the brown dwarf is around 25 times as massive. With two low-mass objects circling at such close range, the scientists wondered if one object could be pulling material from the other. Such a process, known as accretion, is most often seen around objects that are extremely massive, though small in actual size, such as black holes and neutron stars. When a black hole accretes, or draws material from a much smaller nearby object, it pulls the matter around it in a disk. “The difference here is: The thing absorbing matter is not a tiny black hole but a star, which is relatively big in size,” Burdge explains. “So matter just pummels directly onto the surface, at very high speeds, like an asteroid hitting the moon.” The team carried out simulations of possible accretion in ZTF J0440+2325. Taking into account the properties of the star and the brown dwarf, they simulated particles of matter on the brown dwarf, and how these particles should behave within the system over time, according to the laws of physics and equations of motion. “When we track those test particles, we see they indeed fall right onto the surface of the star,” Householder says. “This is the first time we’ve caught a low-mass star actively accreting from another low-mass object.” What’s more, the team calculated that the brown dwarf must be feeding material to its star at a rate of about 1/100,000 of an Earth’s mass each year. That’s about 40 million dump trucks’ worth of material, or roughly 1.3 trillion one-pound burritos every second. While that may seem like a lot of matter to be losing, it is in fact a very small fraction of the brown dwarf. This rate, the researchers estimate, is actually quite slow and steady. Given the size of the system, they say the star could continue leisurely snacking on the brown dwarf, for billions of years. This slow accretion, they say, would resemble a steady stream from the brown dwarf, onto the star. The researchers realized that if they were to view the system from afar, the brightness from the system would chart as a triangle, as the brown dwarf and its stream of matter circles its star. “It’s like you’ve got this continuous fireball onto one of the objects, and as one orbits the other, that hotspot comes in and out of view, and the peak of the triangle signal is when you’re looking right at the fireball,” Burdge explains. With the mystery of the triangle light curve solved, the team hopes to spot similar slow-feeding systems nearby. “It’s inspiring a lot of new searches on our part,” Householder says. “I think we’re going to learn a lot about a different kind of way that planets and brown dwarfs interact with their host stars.” This research was supported, in part, by the National Science Foundation. articles.title: Hooked on tuna: People have been harvesting these ocean predators for 44,000 years
articles.summary: Bones in archaeological sites, ancient rock art, paintings on frescos and vases, written historical records and ethnographic accounts all helped researchers recreate a deep history of people and tuna.
articles.content: Hooked on tuna: People have been harvesting these ocean predators for 44,000 years Skip to content For millennia, people have found ways to locate, catch and share tunas. LUNAMARINA/iStock via Getty Images Plus From a humble mayonnaise-laden sandwich to an expensive piece of sashimi, tuna is a prized source of food for people around the world. Once an inexpensive, easily shipped canned protein source, today’s bluefin tunas can fetch millions of dollars at auction . Millions of tons of tuna are harvested every year, supporting a global industry worth around US$40 billion annually . But tunas are more than just the pink flesh found in cans and sushi, and humanity’s story with these fish goes back further than you might expect. As a biologist and an archaeologist interested in long-term human-environment interactions, we wanted to investigate the deep record of people’s relationship with tunas. We drew on the expertise of 18 leading researchers worldwide and studied a variety of sources, from the skeletal remains of tunas in archaeological sites to ancient rock art, paintings on frescos and vases, written historical records and ethnographic accounts from Indigenous communities. This data helped us understand where, when and why people caught tunas, and what cultural and environmental forces shaped these early fisheries. In turn, this provided new insights into how past harvests compare with the millions of tons caught today. Tunas travel in schools that can include thousands of individual fish. DeepAqua/iStock via Getty Images Plus An apex predator of the ocean “Tuna” is a common name given to a group of 15 fish species . The major market species include eight “true tunas” in genus Thunnus along with skipjack tuna ( Katsuwonus pelamis ). Tunas are among the largest predators in the open ocean, with some species reaching almost 10 feet (over 3 meters) in length and living for over 40 years . Tuna are champion swimmers; Pacific bluefin tuna can migrate 5,000 miles (8,000 kilometers) across the northern Pacific in a matter of months . Tuna are also ecologically important apex predators and serve as sentinels of ocean health . However, most scientific research has focused on the past 75 years, with assessments of the health of tuna populations benchmarked against the year 1950 . The focus on recent decades raises a variety of questions about the deeper history of fishing for tuna prior to the past century. Archaeologists have found the earliest tuna bones harvested by people in Jerimalai Cave in East Timor. Sue O’Connor A deep and dynamic history The oldest definitive evidence of tuna fishing, in the form of skeletal remains of what were likely skipjack tuna, comes from East Timor in southeast Asia about 44,000 years ago . Likely aided by deepwater channels that brought tunas close to shore, this early example of tuna fishing is somewhat unusual – most areas of the world don’t contain evidence of tuna fishing until 10,000 years ago or more recently. Ancient fishers in Japan and Korea, for instance, captured tunas beginning at least 7,000 years ago, with a rich culinary tradition and large-scale harvests that trace their way to the present day love for these fishes in the region. A 13th-century engraving shows tuna traps at Zahara de los Atunes, Spain, where fishers would tighten the net and pull the fish toward shore. Fundación Casa Medina Sidonia The northeastern Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea are home to one of the world’s oldest and most important tuna fisheries, focused on Atlantic bluefin tuna. A few ancient tuna bones found in a Neanderthal site in Gibraltar dating to around 26,000 years ago may have been obtained by Neanderthals scavenging. However, by 9,000 to 11,000 years ago, thousands of tuna bones were deposited in Greece in a cave overlooking Kiladha Bay. The number of sites across Europe with tuna remains increases rapidly in the archaeological record after about 8,000 years ago . These early fishers used a variety of methods to catch tuna , including hook and line, harpoons, and traps or nets. They often took advantage of topographic features where fish could be driven close to shore. This tuna fishing is captured in written records, paintings and other art, showing the cultural importance of these fish to ancient European societies. The ancient Greeks deemed tuna worthy of sacrifice to the gods and used them as offerings to Poseidon . By 3,000 years ago, a commercial Atlantic bluefin tuna fishery had formed in the Mediterranean, with large-scale trade and specialized nets and traps. By the 16th and 17th centuries, people may have caught tens of thousands of tons annually . This fishery was made possible by the predictable migration patterns of Atlantic bluefin and coastal access to tunas – no dangerous oceanic voyages necessary. A Pacific bluefin tuna bone from an archaeological site on Vancouver Island. Iain McKechnie For over 5,000 years, Indigenous people on North America’s northwest coast, particularly in Nuu-chah-nulth territory, had an important and complex fishery for Pacific bluefin tuna . Ethnographic accounts from native elders describe how during unique warm-water events in late summer, people voyaged out at night into the fjords, aided by natural bioluminescent plankton. With spotters overlooking the fjords and communicating from land, fishers set fires in canoes to lure tuna close enough to harpoon. People would spear these massive fish, some perhaps more than 6 feet (2 meters) in length and weighing 640 pounds (290 kilograms). Bluefin tuna vertebrae have been found in 23 regional archaeological sites . In Southern California, people also captured tunas, particularly around Santa Catalina Island, where Indigenous fishers caught Pacific bluefin, yellowfin, albacore and skipjack tunas for 6,000 years, leaving the fishes’ skeletal remains in regional archaeological sites. Workers at a Starkist tuna cannery in 1953 in California. Charles E. Rotkin/Corbis/VCG via Getty Images However, it wasn’t until the 19th and 20th centuries that commercial and sport fisheries for tuna developed in the area. Tuna experienced a meteoric rise in popularity during World War I and World War II. Often centered around canneries in Los Angeles and San Diego, Southern California commercial and industrial tuna fisheries benefited from Japanese and Portuguese immigrant fishing communities, which helped spawn a global industry for tuna. Emergence of oceanic exploitation Tuna consumption by people is obviously nothing new. But how has the scale of tuna harvest changed through time? Using the quantity of tuna bones present in archaeological sites as a rough metric, we found that even the largest of these ancient fisheries – those in the Mediterranean – likely only removed thousands of tonnes of tuna over millennia, which pales in comparison to the millions of tons of tuna now removed from the oceans every year. This contrast brings up important questions: What are the consequences of oceanic exploitation exploding over such a relatively short period of time? How can people sustainably manage tuna populations? There are no easy answers, and three of the commercially important tuna species – southern bluefin, Pacific bluefin and bigeye tuna – remain endangered, vulnerable or near threatened . However, in several regions a combination of effective governance, monitoring and harvest controls have stabilized tuna populations even with intensive harvests. People have shared a long relationship with tuna, not just by harvesting them but also depicting them in art. Heritage Art/Heritage Images/Hulton Archive via Getty Images The deep history of tuna fishing also highlights the human capacity for innovation. For more than 44,000 years, people have found ways to locate, catch and share tunas. That same capacity, channeled into international cooperation and science-based management, may help maintain global tuna stocks at sustainable levels – even if they’ll likely never again reach precommercial fishing levels of abundance. articles.title: The Monte Verde controversy is back: who first lived in the Americas?
articles.summary: The Monte Verde sites in Chile have been the source of arguments among archaeologists for decades. Columnist Michael Marshall finds the row is heating up again – and could change our understanding of the first peoples in the Americas
articles.content: The Monte Verde controversy is back: who first lived in the Americas? | New Scientist Advertisement Subscribe now Illustration of the Monte Verde people Julieta Torres/www.indaga.me This is an extract from Our Human Story, our newsletter about the revolution in archaeology. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every month . In every scientific field, there are totemic places. The CERN physics laboratory that houses the Large Hadron Collider; the Cavendish lab in Cambridge where James Watson and Francis Crick did their research on the structure of DNA; NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California. In archaeology, one such place is a site in Chile called Monte Verde. For half a century, Monte Verde has been central to our understanding of the peopling of the Americas. For two decades, the story that Monte Verde told was wildly controversial. It then became fairly settled, but, as of this year, it has become controversial again. Advertisement The details of the new argument are, at times, punishingly technical, and I’m going to give only the roughest outline of them or we’d be here all week. However, the actual questions at the back of all this are simple: who were the first people to live in the Americas, and when did they arrive? The Americas were the last continents to be settled by humans . (Well, there’s Antarctica, but given it was discovered only within the last 300 years, let’s not worry about it.) The oldest known hominins lived in Africa, and we don’t see hard evidence of hominins anywhere else until 1.8 million years ago , when Homo erectus reached what is now Georgia – the one in Eurasia, not the US state. Later, hominins like Neanderthals and Denisovans spread throughout Eurasia. Later still, our species, Homo sapiens , appeared in Africa and migrated all over Eurasia . That’s a lot of travelling around, over a period of nearly 2 million years. Yet none of those people seem to have reached the Americas. While the exact timing of that momentous landfall is very contentious, we are talking at most about the last 35,000 years – and the main waves of settlement seem to have been between 20,000 and 13,000 years ago. That’s where Monte Verde comes in. It has long been claimed to be the oldest evidence of humans in the Americas – or at least the oldest one with indisputable traces of human intervention and reliable dating evidence. Monte Verde told us that people entered the Americas thousands of years earlier than previously thought. Now, the archaeological data at the site is under attack – and with it, our understanding of the prehistory of the Americas. Read more The genome of a long-extinct ancient human is hiding within us Early Americans The Monte Verde archaeological site sits along Chinchihuapi Creek in Chile Jorge Guzmán and Francisco Donoso Monte Verde is in southern Chile, a few tens of kilometres inland from the Pacific Ocean. To the south, the coast of South America fractures into a confusing scatter of peninsulas and islands. The Andes mountain chain, which runs north-south, lies to the east. Monte Verde sits on a flood plain: it is on the banks of the Chinchihuapi creek, a tributary of the larger Maullín river. Archaeologists have been excavating Monte Verde on and off for almost 50 years, since 1977 . One of the most prominent is Tom Dillehay at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee. He and his colleagues have excavated two relatively close sites, simply dubbed Monte Verde I and Monte Verde II. Monte Verde I is tricky. It contains burned areas and numerous putative stone artefacts – although some may simply be natural stones, albeit unusual ones. Early studies radiocarbon dating the charcoal placed the site as 33,000 years old , which has never been widely accepted. In a 2015 study, Dillehay’s team dated Monte Verde I to between 14,500 and 18,500 years ago . However, because the human traces are so sparse, the older end of that range is disputed, and Dillehay himself doesn’t put too much store by it. Stronger evidence comes from Monte Verde II. Here, the team found artefacts made of stone, wood and bone , as well as what seem to be the foundations for a structure, perhaps a tent. Directly above the layers containing these materials was a layer of peat, which Dillehay’s team dated to 14,500 years ago. This implies that Monte Verde II is at least that old. In 1997, a team of archaeologists visited the site and gave Dillehay’s analyses an official stamp of approval . Subsequent evidence has supported the dating: for instance, in 2008, Dillehay’s team identified marine algae at Monte Verde II, which they directly dated to 14,220 to 13,980 years ago. Tom Dillehay at the Monte Verde archaeological site Jorge Guzmán Dávila/www.indaga.me Today, Dillehay says, the evidence for the age of Monte Verde consists of “more than 1000 radiocarbon and luminescence dates and intact chrono-stratigraphy, as well as diagnostic stone tools dated in other sites”. These finds at Monte Verde II effectively detonated our main ideas around the peopling of the Americas. For much of the 20th century, most archaeologists believed that the first Americans were peopled dubbed the Clovis, after a site in New Mexico. Clovis peoples made distinctive pointed stone tools. The oldest Clovis sites are about 13,000 years old. So strong was the consensus around the Clovis First model that any pre-Clovis site came under immense scrutiny. Sites like Cooper’s Ferry, Buttermilk creek and Paisley caves in North America have been endlessly picked over. Monte Verde was the first site to survive this process and become established. In March this year, another team of archaeologists tried to tear the whole edifice down. Read more Denisovan tools from cave in China show how mysterious humans lived Younger than that Todd Surovell first learned about Monte Verde in 1994, when he was an undergraduate at the University of Wisconsin. Dillehay came as a guest speaker to talk about the site. “I was absolutely blown away,” says Surovell. “It really inspired my career.” Surovell is now an archaeologist at the University of Wyoming. Increasingly sceptical about Monte Verde, Surovell and his colleagues visited the area in 2022 and 2023. They published their results in Science in March 2026 . His team didn’t excavate at Monte Verde I or II, but along the banks of Chinchihuapi creek. Based on the layers of sediments they found, they reconstructed a history of the area. Chinchihuapi Creek cuts through the landscape Jorge Guzman and Francisco Donoso About 20,000 years ago, they say, when Earth’s climate was deep in a glacial period, the region was the outwash from a glacier extending down from the Andes: a plain with braided streams and lots of sand and gravel. Later, as the climate warmed, a forest moved in, transitioned into a wetland, and was then buried – forming a black peat. Then, around 11,000 years ago, a volcano called Michinmahuida erupted and blanketed the area in a layer of ash, called the Lepué Tephra. Afterwards, Chinchihuapi creek cut down through all these layers, forming an exposed surface where people lived. This means that Monte Verde II must be younger than the Lepué Tephra ash layer, Surovell’s team argues. Based on dating of sands and gravels at their excavation sites, they place it between 8200 and 4200 years ago. To say this has caused a row would be an understatement. The Science paper now has seven “eLetters” attached to it, responding to the various claims . On 19 August, Dillehay and his colleagues published an entire paper in the journal PaleoAmerica , rebutting Surovell’s team’s arguments. A central problem with all this is that Surovell’s team excavated near Monte Verde but not actually at it. Or, as Dillehay puts it: “They did not excavate at the site, never saw the stratigraphy and examined only surface landscape from 50 to 4000 meters away in distance.” Because this is a flood plain, where rivers shift over time and sediments can be mixed, extrapolating from one place to another is tricky. For instance, Surovell’s team identified a layer of peat, which they say corresponds to the peat overlaying the Monte Verde II occupational layer. Dillehay’s team says it doesn’t. Likewise, one of the key planks of evidence supporting Monte Verde’s age is the large quantity of wood at the site, which has been dated. “There’s a lot of wood in there that dates to the ice age, but that wood is derived from… older deposits,” argues Surovell. “It was eroded from these older deposits to wash into the stream onto these younger surfaces.” However, Dillehay argues that the wood shows no sign of having been redeposited – for example, there is no telltale damage from being bashed around in flood water. Furthermore, there is no sign of the crucial Lepué Tephra ash layer at Monte Verde II, either above or below the layer with the artefacts. Dillehay argues that, therefore, it can’t tell us anything about the age of the site. And so the argument goes on, for thousands of words and many more lines of reasoning. I have tried to pull out the main points, but I can’t overemphasise how much of a rabbit hole this is. Every detail of Dillehay’s and Surovell’s excavations is being picked over. When a scientific claim becomes disputed, resolving who is correct can become extremely challenging, because of the “experimenter’s regress”. If we don’t know the true answer to some question, then it is difficult to judge whether we have performed an experiment correctly. If you get a surprising result, maybe you have found something new, or maybe you screwed up the experiment. So, if an experiment contradicts your favoured theory about the world, you can simply argue that the experiment was flawed, or that the people who ran it are incompetent. The trouble is that they can say the same thing about your experiment. Hence the experimenter’s regress: a seemingly endless cycle of claim and counterclaim, with each side arguing that the other is stuffing up their research in crucial ways. I’m not in a position to break the cycle here and call the correct answer. For one thing, I don’t feel confident judging whether the peat layer at Monte Verde II and the peat layer Surovell’s team found are, or aren’t, the same thing. Read more Lost civilisation in the Amazon may have numbered 3 million people Pre-Clovis peoples? Were the Clovis people the first to the Americas? Illustration by Eric Carlson in collaboration with archaeologists Ben Potter and James Chatters Can we instead answer the question with independent lines of evidence? As I mentioned, there are now a lot of pre-Clovis sites in the Americas, and more turn up fairly regularly. Some of the most dramatic recent discoveries have been at White Sands National Park in New Mexico, where footprints and drag marks have been found that seem to be about 22,000 years old . Meanwhile, genetic studies of Indigenous Americans and their Asian relatives seem to indicate people moving into the Americas around 15,000 years ago . One interpretation is that there were some early wanderers who didn’t survive , followed by at least one major migration. This would seem to imply that people were in the Americas before the Clovis era, regardless of the truth about Monte Verde. Surovell, for his part, argues that “the evidence for pre-Clovis in North and South America is not very good anywhere” and that “every other one of these sites has been questioned, and every other one of these sites is still in play”. He contends that “there are a heck of a lot of people in my field who you don’t hear from very much in the press”, who think the pre-Clovis sites are too poor in quality to be trusted. “I predict that you’re going to very much see archaeologists increasingly migrating back towards the Clovis First position.” Meanwhile, Dillehay remains confident. “We just finished having an independent group of geologists and archaeologists at the site… who saw the stratigraphy, confirmed our work and pointed out the major errors of Surovell et al,” he says. “They will be publishing the results soon.” I don’t know which of these predictions will prove more prescient, but I will say that I thought this question had largely been settled, and I am interested to see if people like Surovell succeed in reopening it. articles.title: NASA's Roman Space Telescope Takes First Coronagraph Instrument Observation
articles.summary: On September 22, the Coronagraph Instrument on NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope opened its eyes to cosmic light for the first time. The ultimate purpose of the instrument—which is commanded from Caltech's IPAC , a science and data center for astrophysics and planetary sciences—is to demonstrate technology that can block starlight, providing unprecedented views of the planets and dusty disks around nearby stars. The coronagraph first woke up on September 1 and stretched its digital, electronic, and mechanical "limbs" mid-month. Once the Roman team confirmed that the fine-guidance system was holding the Coronagraph Instrument steady, scientists adjusted the focus so it could take its first bleary-eyed look at space, which will help scientists fine-tune the instrument's view. "We're all extremely pleased with how well things are working," says Alexandra Greenbaum , coronagraph data management system lead at IPAC. "There's a lot of collaboration that went into this milestone, so it's wonderful to see all of us working together and to be a part of the team. I'm really looking forward to supporting the rest of commissioning, both on the operations and the data processing." The coronagraph was designed and built by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which Caltech manages for NASA. It will block out a star's light, making the surrounding area dark enough to image the faint light of orbiting planets. These first tests "build toward digging a dark hole on the sky," Greenbaum says. In the future, both the Coronagraph Instrument and the observatory's primary Wide Field Instrument, will undergo further calibrations and tests during a three-month commissioning period. NASA anticipates releasing Roman's first images by early 2027. This first observation "confirms that the instrument can produce a focused image," says Vanessa Bailey, a Roman Coronagraph Instrument scientist at JPL. News AI Gadgets Microsoft’s new AI chip makes it less reliant on Nvidia’s GPUs The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027. The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027. by Tom Warren Oct 12, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Microsoft’s Maia 300 chip. Image: Microsoft Tom Warren is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad , who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years. Microsoft is announcing its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip today, designed to be the “primary AI inference system” for Microsoft’s products and services. Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks. Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” says Scott Guthrie , executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.” These efficiency improvements will allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its in-house AI chips soon, instead of ones from Nvidia and AMD. “We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services,” says Guthrie. Maia 300 chips will start being used for production workloads in 2027. Image: Microsoft Maia 300 is a successor to the 200, which was only announced in January . Maia 200 is already running on production AI workloads across Microsoft, including Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft’s own AI models. “Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real world metrics for AI services,” says Guthrie. “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks.” Related Microsoft is finally making custom chips — and they’re all about AI Microsoft’s latest AI chip goes head-to-head with Amazon and Google Microsoft is using a new chiplet architecture to get its all-important efficiency gains. Built on TSMC’s N2P process node, the latest Maia 300 architecture separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions. “This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” says the Azure hardware and infrastructure team. Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve its goal of catching up with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. “At that scale we need a platform that we own, and that we co-design with our models. That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. articles.title: 'It could have been a very different history': Researchers are finally starting to pin down how many Indigenous people were living in the Americas when Columbus arrived
articles.summary: Archaeologists and geographers have been trying to estimate the pre-1492 population of the Americas for decades. But it's difficult.

Christopher Columbus is depicted as giving gifts to the first Native Americans he met when he landed on what is now called San Salvador. (Image credit: The Washington Post/Getty Images) Copy link Facebook X Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter When Christopher Columbus made landfall in the Americas on Oct. 12, 1492, he encountered Indigenous Lucayans living on the Bahamian island now called San Salvador. Columbus wrote in his diary about " great multitudes of men " who greeted him that day, bartered with him and told him about other groups who lived on nearby islands. But within a few decades after Columbus' arrival, the Indigenous people of the Americas were decimated by what anthropologist Eric Wolf called the " Great Dying " — a combination of epidemic disease, warfare and enslavement that led to a rapid decline in the Native population. For centuries, researchers have been trying to figure out how many Indigenous people lived in the Americas just prior to the fateful arrival of European colonizers. The answer to that question has been surprisingly elusive, and estimates based on historical censuses, archaeological sites and land carrying capacity in the Western Hemisphere have varied wildly. Recent research into Native American demography has revealed that the population peaked several centuries before Europeans showed up on the shores of North America — and that if Europeans had arrived at that peak, the entire history of the continent may have been different. Early estimates of the Indigenous population People have lived in the Americas for at least 14,000 years , having entered the continents via the region around the Bering Strait. Archaeological evidence shows these first Americans dispersed throughout the newly encountered lands fairly quickly. But what happened to the population between that dispersal and the arrival of Columbus is a huge unknown; estimates of the number of Indigenous people living in the Western Hemisphere in 1492 have ranged from 1 million to 112 million people. "We don't have good quantitative estimates," George Milner , an anthropologist at Penn State, told Live Science. "The numbers are all over the place." One of the first modern researchers who attempted to quantify the Indigenous population prior to Columbus was anthropologist Henry Dobyns . In a 1983 book , Dobyns used estimates of how many people each type of landscape could support as well as historical records of 16th-century disease epidemics to arrive at an Indigenous population estimate of around 112 million people — more than 100 times larger than some previous experts had believed. "In essence, Dobyns filled up the landscape to its maximum carrying capacity, so that all environmentally similar places were occupied by the same number of people," Milner said. "He also made the assumption that epidemic disease spread widely and universally, which would make sense if the landscape was filled up." But a burst of archaeological research in the 1970s and 1980s revealed that the Americas were not uniformly settled, Milner said. Dobyns' estimates were therefore much too high. Had Europeans tried settling the continent at A.D. 1000, they would have run into a much, much larger Indigenous population. Robert Kelly, archaeologist at University of Wyoming Researchers then began to focus on creating population estimates for specific regions of the hemisphere, using techniques such as the relative density of pottery sherds at a site, the number of stone tools and flakes, the number and size of houses, and mortality trends from human skeletons. In a 2019 study , geographers compiled 129 population estimates from 82 published studies to model the hemisphere-wide distribution of the Indigenous population in 1492. The researchers split the hemisphere into seven regions — the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, Inca territory, Amazonia, North America and the rest of the Americas — and reached a combined estimate of 60.5 million. Their estimate for North America (modern-day Canada and the U.S.) was about 3 million to 6 million, less than one-third of Dobyns' estimate of 18 million. Native Americans lived in large settlements such as this one at Cahokia Mounds, an archaeological site near modern-day St. Louis, Missouri. (Image credit: The Washington Post/Getty Images) A regional perspective – North America The 2019 study found that the most populous groups in the Western Hemisphere in 1492 were the Aztecs, largely in modern-day Mexico; and the Inca, who lived along the west coast of South America. But the people we know the most about from an archaeological standpoint are Indigenous groups in the U.S. and Canada. In a 2010 study , Milner and geographer George Chaplin zoomed in on the data from eastern North America, compiling historic group sizes and sizes of archaeological occupation areas to estimate the location and size of "population aggregates." Using this method, their overall estimate for the eastern U.S. and southeastern Canada was about 1.6 million people. "Our mean estimates," Milner and Chaplin wrote, "indicate that North America held roughly 2.8 to 5.7 million people" or a "best estimate" of 3.8 million people in the early 16th century, before European diseases dramatically decreased the size of the Indigenous population. "If you want to start estimating specific populations, you should use measures that work across regions," Robert Kelly , an archaeologist at the University of Wyoming, told Live Science. "People produce things that can be carbon-dated everywhere, because everyone had to build fires for heat and for cooking." Charcoal from hearths is one of the main human-made things that archaeologists use to radiocarbon-date a site. The radiocarbon data provides a range of dates showing when the firewood was likeliest to have been used. In North America, many of those carbon-14 dates from charcoal, as well as from animal bones and plant remains from archaeological sites, have been entered into the Canadian Archaeological Radiocarbon Database (CARD). In a 2009 study , Matthew Peros , a geographer at Bishop's University in Quebec, and co-authors mathematically combined the radiocarbon date ranges in CARD to generate a single curve that revealed how common C-14 dates were over time. At the time, CARD had about 25,000 records. Because time periods with more people most likely produced more material that could be carbon-dated, the shape of the radiocarbon date curve gave the team an idea of when the population of North America increased and decreased. They found that the population of North America increased rapidly around 50 B.C. and peaked around A.D. 1150. From that time until European contact, the Indigenous population may have been declining, possibly because of increased mortality from diseases like tuberculosis as people aggregated into denser settlements. In a 2025 study, Kelly and colleagues created a radiocarbon date curve, which revealed a Native American population peak around A.D. 1150. (Image credit: Kelly et al. / PNAS) "The 1150 date was an interesting finding that also surprised us," Peros told Live Science. "I had assumed it would be more like 1500 just following the arrival of the Europeans." In a 2025 study , Kelly and co-authors found a similar temporal peak. By that time, CARD's dataset had ballooned to over 100,000 dates , making the estimate more robust. "Although devastated by European contact, the Indigenous population did not simply increase to a peak at 1500 CE and then decline," the researchers wrote in the study. In fact, they found evidence for a slight recovery in population numbers just prior to 1500. But how large was that population? By combining the radiocarbon date curve with a starting population and factoring in average annual population growth, researchers can estimate the number of people living in North America around 1492, Peros said. In their study, Peros and co-authors assumed that a handful of extended families — around 1,000 people — entered North America about 15,000 years ago as the founder population. With those inputs, the researchers estimated that the maximum population of North America was about 2.5 million in 1150 and had declined to about 1.8 million in 1492. But if people arrived significantly earlier than 15,000 years ago — which might be the case, given evidence from sites like White Sands in New Mexico, which dates to 23,000 years ago — or arrived in greater numbers, those population figures would be even higher. "Had Europeans tried settling the continent at A.D. 1000, they would have run into a much, much larger Indigenous population," Kelly said. At that time, the city of Cahokia , near modern-day St. Louis, encompassed 6 square miles (16 square kilometers) and had a population of nearly 20,000 people. "They could have fielded thousands of warriors, and it would have been a very different experience for the Europeans," Kelly said. "It could have been a very different history ." Why does this matter? Exclusive to Live Science Pro 13,000-year-old butchered bones of long-tusked beast found in Chile give more evidence of early first Americans Ancient DNA reveals mysterious Indigenous lineage that lived in Argentina for nearly 8,500 years — but rarely interacted with others Ancient Indigenous lineage of Blackfoot Confederacy goes back 18,000 years to last ice age, DNA reveals Experts told Live Science that the pre-1492 population of what is now the U.S. and Canada was between 2 million and 4 million. The archaeological deep dive in this region sets up the possibility that a full Western Hemisphere population estimate may be made someday. Milner is optimistic they'll eventually get there. "Will it be done in my lifetime? Probably not," he said. "It's time-consuming, laborious and not especially flashy work to do." Nonetheless, demography is important work, he said, because it can help us make estimates to prepare for the future. "The world's population has more than doubled in my lifetime; that's unheard of in human existence," Milner said. "Environmental scientists are really trying to look at what's happened over long periods of time to give us a range of variation of what might happen in the future. We have to make some informed decisions about how to manage our landscape and accommodate these changes." Understanding the number of Indigenous inhabitants in the Western Hemisphere in 1492 is also key to understanding the history of North America. "North America was not an empty continent when the Europeans arrived," Peros said. "There were people and civilizations pretty much everywhere in the Americas for a long period of time. It is important for people to understand that when we talk about questions of reconciliation and when we do land acknowledgements." Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here . How much do you know about the first people to reach the Americas? Find out with our First Americans quiz! Kristina Killgrove Staff writer Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing. articles.content: Mars may be a hellhole. But the moon is not far behind. | MIT Technology Review Skip to Content Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars. The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements . If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones , robotic landers, communication satellites , and a nuclear power plant ; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water. Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.” The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved? But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher. SELMAN DESIGN But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales. Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán. Will anyone succeed? The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F. Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids. And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs. Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher. NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold. Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant. But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night. But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,” Philip Metzger , a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?” Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle. Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings. Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely. Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions. It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions. The temperature in the moon’s south pole craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night. Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious. And as Stuart George, a physicist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, explains, it comes in two unpleasant forms. The first is galactic cosmic rays , which rain down on the moon almost constantly. “They’re made by supernovas and neutron star mergers—all these kinds of things,” says George. And because the atomic nuclei, protons, and electrons that make them up are moving at significant fractions of the speed of light, these cosmic rays have oodles of kinetic energy, meaning they can punch through thin shielding (say, a metal wall) with ease. “They also have this habit where the heavier ions are fragmenting in that shielding and making secondary particles,” says George. That means if your shield is too thin, the astronauts behind it will be blasted with a surprisingly large dose of radiation. Then you have the sun. It may sustain life on Earth, but without our planet’s thick atmosphere and magnetic bubble to get in its way, moonwalkers will occasionally be blasted by one of its paroxysms: a solar flare (a burst of diverse types of radiation) or a coronal mass ejection (volleys of magnetized plasma). “During Apollo, they knew that if a large solar flare occurred while the crew was on the moon, there would be no way to keep them alive,” says Metzger. The crew could have developed acute radiation sickness and perished in a matter of days. The way to survive a powerful solar flare or coronal mass ejection is straightforward: “Get back inside a habitat where there’s more shielding,” says George—preferably a dedicated, highly shielded “storm shelter,” essentially a thick-walled bunker. The issue is that astronauts might be outside the base, driving a rover many miles away. Coronal mass ejections take hours to days to reach the vicinity of the Earth-moon system, but solar flares can do so in under an hour. And scientists can’t yet model the sun well enough to give much advance notice. “All of the capability to forecast solar storms is kind of like where weather forecasting [was] … in the ’50s and ’60s,” says George. As for those punchy galactic cosmic rays, the only way to avoid them would be to put a lot of stuff—lunar rocks, possibly—between the astronauts and the sky. “Build habitat modules underground,” says Chris Dreyer , director of engineering at the Center for Space Resources at the Colorado School of Mines. One option: Burrow living quarters into lava tubes, the naturally hollowed-­out volcanic tunnels created by molten rock eons ago. At this point, NASA hasn’t mentioned any plans to make its moon base subterranean, but it may need to if it wants to end up with a small lunar city. Radiation limits the time astronauts can spend on the lunar surface over their entire life—it can total around two years max, experts estimate, before the health risk becomes too high. Unfortunately, that’s not all space will throw at them. When the Artemis II astronauts swung around the far side of the moon earlier this year, they saw curious flashes light up the silvery land below. These were the explosive deaths of small meteoroids punching into the lunar surface. Earth is naturally protected from smaller space rocks, up to around 50 feet in diameter: They burn up inconsequentially in the atmosphere. “You don’t have that option on the moon,” says Philip Lubin , a physicist and planetary defense researcher at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Since smaller rocks plunge toward planets and moons far more frequently than larger ones do, this means the moon is often peppered by what are effectively tiny space bullets. They could easily puncture a spacesuit or the engine of a moon rover. How do you protect astronauts from the onslaught? “The simplest answer is burial,” says Nicholas Schmerr , a planetary seismologist at the University of Maryland—conveniently, the same way you’d deal with radiation exposure. Pile up moon rocks onto your base walls or put habitable structures in lava tubes. Inconveniently, there’s always a chance that a bigger asteroid will come along. Even buried habitation modules would have trouble surviving an assault from a 50-footer—about the length of a semi-trailer. That doesn’t mean a moon base would be helpless against bigger asteroids. Planetary defense has come a long way in just a few decades. NASA’s DART mission demonstrated that it could deflect an asteroid by ramming into the rock with an uncrewed spacecraft, and cutting-­edge experiments at clandestine labs around the US suggest that a nuclear bomb could swat away or entirely vaporize errant space rocks. An array of both ground-based and space-based telescopes specifically designed to spy killers —such as the ATLAS quartet of largely automated telescopes, and the soon-to-be-launched NEO Surveyor infrared telescope—are also aiming to find 90% of the near-Earth asteroids potentially capable of wiping out entire cities (those 460 feet across) in the coming years. All these protections apply to the moon. But asteroids 50 feet across are so stealthy that even NASA’s best telescopes would struggle to see them years or even months in advance. Odds are that they would first be seen not long before they were due to hit the lunar surface. Then what? It’s not unreasonable to imagine several turret-like launch sites on the moon that, owing to the lower gravity and airless environment, could rapidly fire projectiles toward an incoming asteroid. Hit it hard enough and it would break into fragments. Just make sure you shoot when it is as far away as possible: “If you were to break something up into a thousand pieces, then you have a thousand impacts on the moon,” says Lubin. “That might be worse than letting it hit one place.” Having your base destroyed by an asteroid would be awful. But a moon base is far more likely to be imperiled by dust—which, unlike asteroids, is everywhere, all the time. Volcanic lunar rocks, when broken down, turn into sharp, electrostatically charged, adhesive, acrid, abrasive particles. While on the moon, Apollo astronauts who inhaled some of this dust occasionally suffered from a strange “lunar hay fever,” which irritated their eyes and agitated their lungs. That same dust ate through all kinds of gear with disturbing ease. “It rips up seals, gears, motors, spacesuits, habitats—everything else it comes into contact with,” says Justin Cyrus, the CEO of Lunar Outpost, a spaceflight technology company that is providing NASA with one of the Artemis program’s moon rovers. NASA has already developed a defense against these dark shards: the electrodynamic dust shield , or EDS. The lightweight electrodes that make up this shield—which can be layered on machinery, walls, and perhaps even spacesuits—use opposing currents to blast away the electrically charged dust. The EDS worked wonders when tested in labs on Earth, and it also demonstrated its anti-dust magic when sent to the lunar surface in 2025 as part of a NASA-sponsored robotic mission. Amy Fritz, a dust-mitigation researcher at Johnson Space Center, says that the EDS will likely be widely featured all over a lunar habitat. But other dust-fighting instruments are being developed too—including a lint-roller-type object inspired by gecko skin and a sci-fi-esque blaster that uses ionized nitrogen gas. Its first spray will neutralize the charge of the dust to remove its stickiness; then a second burst will clear it off the surface. Irritatingly, the busier a base gets, the dustier things will become. As it expands to the size of a small city, rocket ships will need to deliver cargo and crew to the lunar surface on a frequent cadence. Each takeoff and landing will launch a salvo of dust in every direction, inundating the base’s infrastructure. “You have to worry about essentially being sandblasted every time,” says Fritz. Metzger calculates that even with landing pads more than 3,000 feet away from a base, just 10 to 20 liftoffs or landings would be sufficient to severely damage things like protective coatings on exterior walls and communications equipment. After a while, he says, “everything breaks.” Even if the moon base of the future is buried partly below ground, barricaded against micrometeorites and space radiation, and well equipped with dust-repelling technologies, it’s still a risky gig for any astronaut. Skipping around in a preternaturally agile way at one-sixth of Earth’s gravity will be entertaining. But “microgravity is not good for the human body,” says Dreyer. Muscle wastage, cardiovascular troubles, respiratory problems, and immune deficiencies can arise. Radiation, too, may always afflict lunar residents. And there’s also evidence that disease-causing microbes could stealthily sneak aboard spacecraft, even after stringent sterilization procedures. Those microbes may behave differently than they do on Earth; microgravity experiments (both real and simulated ) have suggested that some become more aggressive and more likely to cause disease . “We call them the invisible crew,” says Lisa Carnell, the director of NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division. The lunar south pole, which is thought to contain a sizable amount of water, is an attractive target for lunar exploration and, eventually, settlement. This map shows the topography of the region. The South Pole–Aitken basin (blue) is an immense crater studded with smaller craters. The vertical distance from the lowest-lying regions to the surrounding peaks can exceed 15 kilometers, almost twice the height of Mount Everest. NASA/GSFC/MIT Hoping to find a better way to protect astronauts, Carnell spearheaded an experiment called AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response), which launched aboard the Artemis II mission. It used thumb-drive-size chips, containing cells taken from the heart, lungs, or other parts of the body, that could be switched on to act like miniature organs. Scientists have previously used this organ-on-a-chip technology for purposes like testing out new pharmaceuticals in a highly controlled setting. For Artemis II, Carnell’s crew sent up chips containing bone marrow samples taken from the mission’s four astronauts. Bone marrow makes red and white blood cells, as well as platelets—the sort of stuff that affects almost the entire human body. So seeing how space radiation and microgravity affect it would give Carnell and her team vital insight into how astronauts’ biology might change on the moon. The advantage of organ chips is that you can make them for any astronaut and then send them into space ahead of time to see how that person’s organs will react to spaceflight. Researchers envision that data from such chips will be able to clue medics in to the specific preventive treatments or pharmaceuticals that will help moonbound astronauts on their journey. What is NASA likely to send up sooner rather than later? “Brain organoids,” says Carnell. Yes, she adds—that sounds super weird. But it would be good to know how a real brain might respond to being on the moon for several months before people start living there. Okay. Your vast moon base and its inhabitants are protected—as much as is possible—from the treacherous lunar environment. But astronauts’ time is extremely valuable, and humans are fragile creatures. You can’t make them do all the heavy lifting, which means that whether you’re trying to make a tiny lunar outpost or a small city, you’re going to need a lot of robots. “The buildup of the moon base, in the first years, will pretty much 99% be robotic,” says NASA’s García-Galán. Autonomy will be there right from the start. NASA’s new version of the moon buggy, its Lunar Terrain Vehicle , can be driven by the astronauts riding in it but can also be piloted remotely from Earth (or from elsewhere on the moon). There are visions, too, of adding modular robotic arms, towing vehicles, and cargo movers—all still in the preliminary stages of planning. Over the next few decades, though, we’ll likely want an army of robots to do our bidding: excavators to dig up lunar rocks that could be turned into concrete and bricks, plus other robots to flatten surfaces, dig trenches, create building foundations, pave landing pads, and build up dust-deflecting berms to keep the base from being sandblasted by launches and landings. Even solar panels and wiring can potentially be made from moon rocks—something that the spaceflight company Blue Origin demonstrated in labs on Earth in 2023 using a geologic simulant designed to match the composition of lunar regolith. Powering this robot army will require considerable energy. Two-week-long nights make solar power an impractical solution. Aside from a cornucopia of high-­capacity, extreme-temperature-resistant batteries, nuclear power is probably the only viable option. A small, car-size nuclear reactor, filled with an almost literal handful of uranium, could power a small village for a decade without needing to be refueled. And although nobody’s yet tested a nuclear reactor on the moon , few doubt that NASA and the US Department of Energy can conjure up a working design—one that perhaps wouldn’t be too different from those aboard nuclear submarines. A moon base in 2100 would probably feature multiple small, autonomously or remotely operated nuclear reactors, which—conveniently—the base-expanding robots could simply plug themselves into to recharge. But the biggest lunar question mark might be water, which planners want to support the astronauts—and to make fuel to launch things from the lunar surface. A process known as electrolysis, which uses electricity to snap apart molecular bonds, can be used to split water into oxygen and hydrogen, both of which could be used to make rocket fuel. Getting them this way could be far less expensive than sending either all the way from Earth. And as an added bonus, it would provide a source of breathable oxygen. Orbital data has revealed that there is some amount of water preserved in patches on the lunar south pole, but little is known about how much there actually is, what form it takes, or how easy it will be to extract. Will there be solid sheets of ice here and there, ready for us to excavate? Or will there be scattered ice crystals intermingled among the rocky grains, requiring some more inventive form of extraction? A lot of the moon’s water is thought to be hiding in deep, dark craters on the south pole, where the environment is so extreme that robots may freeze up, tumble over, or lose contact with the base. “To me, that is the biggest hurdle,” says Paul van Susante, principal investigator of the Planetary Surface Technology Development Lab at Michigan Technological University. Van Susante’s lab has been putting various construction robots through their paces in moon-like vacuum chambers filled with moon-like rocks. His team was part of NASA’s recent Break the Ice challenge , which invited engineers to build robots to test different ways to excavate such rocks. Some teams used an electric jackhammer and a scoop, while others used scrapers to peel off layers of the ground. The teams simulated the moon’s weak gravity using a crane to lift and offset the weight of the robots. Progress in this regard is speeding along. “I won’t say that’s solved, but we’ve got a lot of the puzzle pieces,” says van Susante. Mining the water will be just one part of an extensive operation. “When you extract it, it’s not going to be clean. It needs to be purified,” says Jessica Atkin, a space botanist at Texas A&M. The technology to do this already exists and works fine on terra firma. But things in space never go the way you expect. “There’s a water purification system on the International Space Station (ISS), and it is known for getting contaminated with microbes,” she says. SELMAN DESIGN But if you purify the water sufficiently—something that can handily be achieved on Earth but may falter in microgravity, where fluids flow in stranger ways—then your moon base can hit its stride. With an effective water recycling system, an increasingly populous base will never go thirsty—and, just maybe, you’ll have a lunar greenhouse. Several edible plants have been successfully grown aboard the ISS, including lettuce, mustard greens, tomatoes, and peppers. Lunar dust unfortunately makes for a terrible garden: It’s filled with far too much aluminum—and it forms a resistant layer when watered. But Atkin has shown that with the help of fertilizing fungi, chickpeas can grow in soil much like the volcanic stuff found on the moon. Moon base inhabitants of 2100 would be supported largely by prepacked meals sent from Earth. But in time, they would start growing some of their own produce—probably with a good deal of automation for lighting, watering, and maintenance of humidity and other environmental conditions. Aside from chickpeas, there might also be plenty of lunar tomatoes. They’d be desirable not least because they’ve been bioengineered to produce higher levels of compounds called anthocyanins that, according to some studies, might help humans mitigate the cellular damage caused by space radiation. A garden on the moon would do more than just provide food, as recent experiences on the ISS suggest. Carnell says that NASA recently caught the astronauts aboard the space station doing something sneaky. All plants up there are supposed to be confined to their growth chambers. But “we learned that the crew were pirating our leftover soil and bringing their seeds and planting their own little gardens, if you will, and hiding them in their own cabins,” she says. Conversations were had in the summer of 2026, after which NASA decided to let astronauts grow their own mini-gardens anywhere they wanted. “Some of the astronauts said they thrived better,” says Carnell. Nature, and gardening, has a hugely beneficial psychological effect on those kept in confined quarters hanging above Earth. That will be even truer for those living in lava tunnels under the lunar surface. “That human element is so important,” she says. Nobody is deluded into thinking there isn’t a mountain of technological challenges in the way. Mars may be a hellhole, as the writer Shannon Stirone put it in 2021 in The Atlantic , but the moon isn’t too far behind. It’s an almost comically menacing place to be. Much about it stands in the way of building a safe, self-sustaining, robotically managed base. NASA wants to put the first nuclear reactor on the moon by 2030. China, partnering with Russia, wants to place its own nuclear power plant up there around 2035. Beyond the first basic habitation module, it will take decades of experimentation and iteration on the lunar surface to get to a working moon base spanning hundreds of square miles. But few doubt that with enough time and tinkering, humanity can prevail. “It’s not an unsolvable problem,” says the University of Maryland’s Schmerr. The chief obstacle, especially in the initial stages of building, may be one of political will. NASA is currently bringing every resource to bear on the project—something that the agency hopes could culminate in a small lunar city by the century’s end. But will that commitment continue over multiple US administrations? Will the international community also throw its weight behind the NASA-led effort? NASA has “a very ambitious plan,” says Yuqi Qian , a lunar geologist at the University of Hong Kong. “We need to keep an eye on it.” In fact, he says, “the current plan looks over-ambitious.” The agency, for example, wants to put the first nuclear reactor on the moon by 2030. (China, partnering with Russia, wants to place its own nuclear power plant up there around 2035.) “These sorts of projects—although very exciting, and potentially transformative for humankind—are the first ones to be delayed or scrapped,” says Middleburgh of the Nuclear Futures Institute. NASA’s direction tends to change when a new administration comes into power—sometimes dramatically so. But several experts outside of NASA agree that, at least for now, there is definite momentum and political will behind the moon base. “NASA has very clearly expressed where they want to go, what their priorities [are], what their ambition is, and how they want to do it,” says ESA’s Aschbacher. “It was quite impressive to see.” Even if the political will behind the US-led endeavor is maintained over the coming decades, expanding anywhere beyond an initial, compact moon base will require more than government funding. “There has to be a lunar economy for this to be self-sustaining,” says Dreyer, the space resources expert. Perhaps that will come from the production of rocket fuel, or from the mining of valuable materials on the moon that can replace similar, polluting activities on Earth. But it’s not at all clear how valuable, or not, a lunar economy will be. Even Isaacman, NASA’s chief, doesn’t think the moon will be a major moneymaker. “I don’t know of anything on the moon right now that’s going to be easier and more affordable to mine, manufacture, and then bring back to Earth than what we could make here on Earth,” he remarked back in February. (Instead, he suspects, mining metals from asteroids will be the path to prosperity.) What if, instead, a moon base earns the right to exist because it’s a place for novel scientific research? Aschbacher imagines it will be like humanity’s outposts in Antarctica. Down there, in what truly feels like another world, scientist-explorers work in a land of gleaming and endless ice to learn more about our planet’s climate, its deep past, and its resilient life-forms. “We understand planet Earth by looking into those remote places,” he says. The moon offers a similar opportunity. What discoveries await astronauts in those primordial lava tubes? What will lunar astronomers see in the night sky—with effectively no atmosphere or light pollution in the way—that those on Earth can’t? As in all spaceflight programs, technologies developed up there will no doubt be tweaked to be used back on Earth. And a base on the moon will make exploring the rest of the solar system easier. Technologically, physiologically, and psychologically, the moon “is a proving ground for the technologies we need for Mars,” says NASA’s García-Galán. If we play the US-China race forward, perhaps the lunar south pole of 2100 will feature several sprawling bases operated by multiple geopolitical rivals. Perhaps it’ll be an off-world powder keg of militarized territorial ambitions and jingoism. But maybe it could instead become an international cathedral to science—and the ultimate adventure destination. “Even if countries on planet Earth have difficulty talking to each other,” says Aschbacher, they might behave differently when it comes to the moon. “I’m pretty sure they will get together and see what we can do together, and see what problems we can solve.” After all, he says, up there, far from home, “you’re so dependent on each other.” Robin George Andrews is an award-winning science journalist and doctor of volcanoes based in London. He regularly writes about the Earth, space, and planetary sciences and is the author of two critically acclaimed books: Super Volcanoes (2021) and How to Kill an Asteroid (2024) .
